Her framework crosses listening and speaking with sounds, words, interaction and mental models. These layers are interdependent and evolve over a call, so strong speech recognition alone cannot guarantee task success. She recommends using this structure to diagnose an agent and references ServiceNow’s EVA end-to-end benchmark. The central evaluation contribution is a systematic error taxonomy connected to escalation, abandonment, silent failures and the user’s evolving understanding.
takeaways: Classify failures across listening, speaking, interaction and intent tracking.
Evaluate accumulated conversation experience rather than isolated speech components.
Include user adaptation, clarification and mental-model consistency in diagnosis.
reason: Central topic is structured voice-agent failure analysis, with an end-to-end benchmark reference.

title: 5 Voice Agent Failure Modes You'll Hit in Week One — Venky B, Plivo
summary: Venky B organizes production voice failures into latency, brittle transcription, data collection, speech normalization and turn-taking problems. He discusses measuring time to first audio and balancing model capability, cost and response speed, including multilingual tokenization effects. The most concrete evaluation recommendation is to model collected information as typed fields with validators and confirmations, then test each field independently instead of running expensive end-to-end conversations to discover a broken input. He reports substantial data-collection improvements without fine-tuning through this structural approach. Proper nouns, code-switching, relative dates and pronunciation are practical stress cases. The talk emphasizes engineering reliable subcomponents rather than repeatedly tweaking prompts and hoping compliance improves.
takeaways: Treat collected phone numbers, names and dates as typed, validated fields.
Use field-level regression tests to localize failures before end-to-end testing.
Benchmark multilingual latency and pronunciation on realistic domain vocabulary.
reason: Central failure taxonomy with explicit field-level eval methodology and practical stress tests.

title: The Transcript Looked Fine. The Call Wasn't. — Debugging Voice Agents, Arize
summary: This Arize talk argues that transcripts alone conceal important voice-agent failures: pauses, overlapping speech, transcription errors, tone, and incorrect downstream actions. An AI-generated refund example illustrates a misheard order number, dead air, and a refund issued for the wrong order despite superficially reassuring text. The presenter advocates linking audio, transcripts, tool spans, and multi-turn sessions through normalized OpenInference conventions. Audio-aware evaluations should measure time to first audio, interruptions, sentiment, transcription drift, and actual task success, with results attached to relevant spans. The closing vision extends observation into agent-led diagnosis, replay-based fix validation, and reviewable pull requests; this self-healing workflow is presented as a future direction rather than proven end-to-end performance.
takeaways: Evaluate original audio alongside transcripts and actual tool outcomes.
Stitch turns into sessions to diagnose latency and interruption behavior.
Replay failures against proposed fixes and inspect measured results before approval.
reason: Substantial treatment of voice-agent evaluation and debugging. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
summary: Stephanie Jarmak argues that agent evaluation should resemble a controlled experiment. She shows that changing the harness alone can move benchmark performance by more than thirty percentage points, so a score cannot be attributed to the model without accounting for configuration. Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates; product decisions require realistic local tasks, repeated runs, appropriate measures, and full-pipeline traces. She discusses balancing retrieval precision and recall, enforcing quality gates that actually stop work, and budgeting the human workload created by alarms. Agent-maintained records may be unreliable evidence. Production feedback ultimately tests whether offline improvements survive real conditions, and escalation should be designed around risk rather than a single aggregate success rate.
takeaways: Control harness and environment variables when comparing models.
Repeat realistic tasks and inspect trajectories, not only scores.
Make gates enforceable and account for the human cost of false alarms.
reason: Core: controlled agent experiments, benchmark interpretation, observability, and production validation.

title: Can AI Understand a Distressed Credit? - Harneet Kaur, Axim Intelligence
summary: Harneet Kaur asks how to assess AI reasoning when the final outcome has not happened yet. In a live distressed-credit case involving iHeartMedia, frontier models given similar context initially assign sharply different bankruptcy probabilities. She decomposes the work into extraction, derivation, judgment, and prediction so that factual inputs and assumptions can be checked separately. Structured context and layer-by-layer evaluation bring the models toward a common answer, but she explicitly questions whether convergence proves correctness. Historical testing also risks look-ahead bias. The talk’s contribution is a framework for exposing intermediate reasoning failures and assumptions, not evidence that consensus can validate an uncertain investment forecast.
takeaways: Evaluate extraction and derivation separately from judgment and prediction.
Check assumptions when no final ground truth is available.
Do not confuse agreement between models with independent correctness.
reason: Core: layered reasoning evaluation and validation limits for uncertain financial predictions.

title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
summary: Luke Alvoeiro presents Factory's Missions architecture, emphasizing verification as the mechanism that sustains long-running coding agents. An orchestrator defines features, milestones, and a validation contract before implementation. Workers execute tasks with clean contexts and provide structured handoffs containing commands, exit codes, and unresolved issues. Separate validators run conventional checks and feature reviews, then exercise the live application through user-like interactions. Failures generate corrective work at milestone boundaries. The talk favors serial feature execution with parallel read-only operations and assigns models by role. A Slack-clone example illustrates repeated validation failures and follow-up work, rather than treating passing unit tests as sufficient evidence of completion.
takeaways: Define behavioral correctness during planning, independently of the implementation, and map every required assertion to work.
Separate implementation from fresh-context scrutiny and live user-flow testing to reduce confirmation bias.
Record commands, exit codes, unresolved issues, and corrective work in structured handoffs at validation boundaries.
Parallelize read-only investigation and review selectively rather than allowing concurrent writers to undermine correctness.
reason: Despite the broader multi-agent architecture framing, independent verification is a substantial central mechanism: prewritten acceptance contracts, separate validators, end-to-end behavioral testing, failure-driven corrective tasks, and recorded execution evidence. This is directly relevant to agent testing and verification.
focus: Independent agent verification and behavioral acceptance contracts

title: Anthropic Workshop: Build Agents That Run for Hours — Ash Prabaker & Andrew Wilson
summary: Prabaker and Wilson examine long-running agents through context management, planning, and unreliable self-assessment. Their central pattern separates a generator from an adversarial evaluator that exercises live applications with browser tools rather than merely reviewing code. Subjective design quality becomes an explicit, example-calibrated rubric, while generator and evaluator negotiate testable contracts before implementation. A game-building comparison illustrates how interactive verification exposes broken behavior that superficial completeness and unit tests miss. Trace reading identifies where model judgment diverges from human expectations and guides prompt revisions. Q&A clarifies that evaluators should judge outputs without inheriting generator reasoning, and that rubric scores are useful within runs but not readily comparable across products.
takeaways: Separate builder and critic contexts; have the critic exercise the running application rather than accept the builder's account of success.
Translate subjective preferences and feature requirements into calibrated rubrics and granular, negotiated acceptance tests.
Read complete traces to find judgment failures and revise prompts; reevaluate which harness components remain necessary as models change.
Treat the demonstrated pattern primarily as a greenfield approach requiring project-specific validation, not as evidence of comparable scores across products.
reason: Evaluation and verification are substantial mechanisms of the proposed harness, not passing benchmark references: independent critics perform interactive tests, apply calibrated rubrics, negotiate acceptance contracts, and drive trace-based error analysis. The Q&A also addresses evaluator context contamination and limits of measurement comparability.

title: Spec-Driven Testing for Agents With A Brain the Size of A Planet — Steven Willmott, SafeIntelligence
summary: Steven Willmott argues that an agent specification must contain more than input/output examples. It should explicitly state rules, domain ontologies, terminology, rights, roles and robustness requirements, independently of implementation. Larger models can understand more malicious instructions and broader tool access creates additional attack surface, so capability is not equivalent to safety. The same specification can guide security testing and valid input variations such as typos or rephrasings. Tests should survive framework or model changes and feed iterative repairs. The talk stresses that generating meaningful variants requires knowing which substitutions preserve domain meaning and permissions.
takeaways: Specify rules, role permissions and valid perturbations, not only happy-path examples.
Keep evaluation specifications independent of the deployed framework.
Use domain context to target both security boundaries and robustness tests.
reason: Agent specification, testing, robustness and security validation are central.

title: Agents Building Agents - Alfonso Graziano, Nearform
summary: Alfonso Graziano separates a coding agent that builds software from the product agent being evaluated. A golden dataset and scorers establish the baseline; an optimization loop proposes one hypothesis, edits prompts, tools or code, reruns evaluations and retains or rolls back changes. Reports and memory preserve unsuccessful experiments as well as gains. A second workflow collects production traces with user or expert feedback, clusters failure modes, validates them with domain experts and adds confirmed cases to regression coverage. The talk warns against letting the optimizing agent change datasets or scorers simply to make scores improve.
takeaways: Give builder agents access to traces, explicit metrics and protected evaluation targets.
Retain experiment reports and roll back regressions.
Turn validated production failure clusters into golden-dataset cases.
reason: Evaluation-driven development and production error-analysis workflows dominate the talk.
focus: Evaluation-driven agent improvement and error clustering

title: Frontier results, on device - RL Nabors, Arize
summary: RL Nabors demonstrates selecting small local models through application-specific capability evaluations rather than public reputation. A thread-summarization case uses a golden dataset, deterministic checks for JSON, references and length, plus an LLM judge for factual consistency and latency measurements. The process prototypes with a capable remote model, tests smaller alternatives, and isolates prompt changes one variable at a time. Inspecting individual failures exposes overly strict judging and format problems better handled by post-processing. The resulting model and prompt are retained as regression tests so future migrations cannot silently undo quality or responsiveness gains.
takeaways: Build task-specific golden examples and define success before choosing a model.
Inspect judge disagreements and individual outputs instead of trusting aggregate scores.
Test prompt variants independently and preserve the winning setup as regression coverage.
reason: Detailed capability-eval workflow, golden data, judging and regression tests.

title: The Agentic AI Engineer - Benedikt Sanftl, Mutagent
summary: Benedikt Sanftl and Burak describe automating the offline and online loops of agent engineering. Specifications establish responsibilities and success criteria; evaluation datasets and metrics evolve from real failures rather than appearing complete at the start. Evaluators inspect context completeness, tool outputs, trajectories and harness effects, favoring actionable binary criteria and calibrated judges over ambiguous scores. Production diagnosis groups failures by root cause and derives new tests before optimization. The demo produces trace-linked explanations, assumptions and candidate remedies for human decisions, while sampling and learned indicators reduce the cost of repeatedly reading large trace collections.
takeaways: Treat the evaluation suite as a discovered, growing specification.
Require actionable criteria and judge-variance control.
Turn diagnosed root causes into new tests before applying remedies.
reason: Evaluation-driven development, judge calibration and trace diagnosis are central.

title: What Does Done Even Mean? Agents and Paperclip's Liveness Model - Dotta, Paperclip
summary: Dotta argues that “done” must represent a bundle of operational claims rather than an agent-controlled Boolean. An artifact may exist without being reviewed, independently verified, authorized for release, or proven under real-world conditions. Paperclip’s liveness model balances productive progress against verification through explicit transitions, blockers, reviewers, approvers, watchdogs, and bounded loops. The proposed completion record includes scope, rubric, evidence, verifier, approval authority, residual risk, and next action. Dotta recommends separating author and verifier, often across models, and giving agents practical tools such as browsers and screenshots to demonstrate completion. The central goal is replacing approval theater with inspectable evidence and clear custody.
takeaways: Define completion with explicit scope, standards, evidence, and remaining risk.
Separate the producer from the verifier and authorized approver.
Keep workflows moving with bounded loops and meaningful blockers.
reason: Direct completion-evaluation protocols, evidence requirements, independent verification, and quality contracts.

title: Your Agents Need a Save Button - Hamza Tahir, ZenML
summary: Hamza Tahir distinguishes read-only traces from durable execution checkpoints that preserve code, artifacts, environment, and intermediate state. With checkpoints, teams can replay a production run from a chosen decision, change a model or tool result, and compare outcomes against the original. A Kitaru demonstration extends individual replays into cohort-level analysis of support cases, showing why a cheaper model that looks acceptable once may fail across a meaningful distribution. Tahir warns against optimizing token cost without task value or shipping after one or two examples. His proposed loop is checkpoint, replay, diff, and decide, using representative production cohorts and retaining human approval.
takeaways: Preserve executable state so production failures can become controlled experiments.
Change one factor and compare against a common checkpoint baseline.
Evaluate cohorts and resolved-task value rather than one successful cheap replay.
reason: Direct production-state replay, model/tool comparisons, cohort evaluation, and decision gating.
focus: Checkpoint replay and counterfactual agent evaluation

title: Perception Agents — Antje Barth, Amazon AGI Lab
summary: Antje Barth argues that computer-use capability is insufficient without observing whether actions actually achieved the intended result. She introduces open-source perception-agent components for shared visual annotation and verification against design specifications. The verification demonstration checks rendered appearance, brand and layout rules, and actual application flows such as adding or deleting tasks, then produces a pass/fail report for human review. Shared screen context and precise annotations reduce ambiguous instructions, while a meeting-transcript example feeds requested changes directly into implementation and verification. The talk is a product-pattern demonstration rather than a calibrated benchmark, but its central concern is closing the observe-act-check loop for reliable agent work.
takeaways: Check rendered results and user flows after actions, not merely successful tool calls.
Make design expectations explicit and generate inspectable pass/fail reports.
Use shared visual context to make human feedback more precise.
reason: Core semantic match: visual and user-flow verification harness, self-testing, and explicit checks.

title: Persona Engineering: A Field Guide to AI Synthetic Personas — Ishan Anand, InsightSciences.ai
summary: Ishan Anand frames synthetic personas as bounded forecasts, not replacements for people. He reviews research on interview-grounded personas, prompting, fine-tuning, and mapping free-text responses onto survey distributions. Failure modes include invented contextual confounders, strong option-order sensitivity, amplified demographic bias, and weaker prediction of behavior than stated attitudes. Evaluation must compare synthetic responses with human ground truth using both correlation and distribution-shape metrics. Repeated synthetic sampling does not create additional statistical significance. Anand recommends estimating human inconsistency through retesting or repeated data splits; he cites a study's 83% alignment as normalized against human noise. Synthetic personas can extend existing research, but require empirical calibration and continuing reality checks.
takeaways: Ground personality, context, and experimental conditions explicitly so the model does not invent confounding variables.
Stress-test rewordings, reordered choices, and adversarial challenges, then validate each construction against real human responses.
Measure distribution shape as well as correlation; matching averages can conceal collapsed variation.
Estimate the human-data noise baseline and do not mistake more synthetic samples for stronger real-world statistical evidence.
reason: It provides focused failure analysis, robustness tests, distributional metrics, and human-noise calibration for evaluating synthetic personas.

title: Memory Harnesses for Long-Running Research Agents — Stefania Druga, Sakana.ai
summary: Stefania Druga evaluates local research-agent memory as a write-manage-read control loop, holding the model fixed while varying recall policies. Conditions include no memory, vector retrieval, a ranked decision ledger, and an oracle supplying the correct memory. A literature-review task already fitting in context gains no capability from added memory, only cost. For longer-horizon XBench tasks, she reports that ranked ledger recall performs best across tested conditions, with additional ablations and SpiderV2 experiments. Importantly, oracle retrieval does not guarantee correct answers because a model may ignore or misuse supplied evidence. She argues for evaluating recall policy and token cost explicitly, while noting local hardware and serial-inference constraints.
takeaways: Hold the model fixed when comparing memory policies so improvements can be attributed to the harness.
Include both a no-memory baseline and an oracle-memory condition to diagnose retrieval versus evidence-use failures.
Test beyond the context window; memory can add cost without value when all evidence already fits.
Compare structured ranked recall with vector retrieval and gating, measuring token expenditure alongside correctness.
reason: Presents controlled memory-policy comparisons, oracle baselines, ablations, and cost-aware diagnosis of long-horizon agent failures.

title: Context Engineering in 2026 — Louis-François Bouchard, Omar Solano & Samridhi Vaid, Towards AI
summary: The Towards AI team evaluates context-management strategies for its tutoring agent using real student questions, synthetic multi-turn recall probes, deterministic retrieval checks, and LLM grading. They compare fixed configurations while logging cost, latency, caching, and whether compaction actually triggered. Contrary to their initial defaults, retaining history often beats summarization or clearing tool outputs, which can destroy cache reuse and force retrieval again. The speakers report roughly 95% detail recall with full history versus 32% after summarization, while acknowledging limited trials in the initial experiments. Local context limits change the trade-off: hybrid retrieval helps oversized documents, but chat memory remains weaker. Their selected setup uses cached DeepSeek V4 Flash, hybrid retrieval, and a compaction threshold.
takeaways: Check that the intervention actually triggers; single-turn tests may never exercise compaction.
Measure cache hit rate, retrieval repetition, latency, and recall together rather than optimizing token count alone.
The team's filesystem-browsing tool added latency without improving recall on its tested student questions.
Distinguish long chat memory from document retrieval, and interpret small-trial results as workload-specific evidence.
reason: Provides explicit evaluation tasks, intervention checks, controlled comparisons, and measured quality-cost trade-offs for context engineering.

title: Don’t be data poor — Anuj Iravane, Anterior
summary: Anuj Iravane describes building healthcare evaluation datasets when contracts prohibit retaining patient records or derivative copies. Anterior reverses its policy-guided inference task: sample an outcome and a symbolic policy reasoning trace, then generate supporting records. A coarse-to-fine pipeline creates patient invariants, journeys, encounter plans, and documents, followed by consistency checks and round-trip validation against the intended label. Clinicians can steer generation and own pipeline logic through skills, allowing realistic failure cases without engineering changes. Iravane says synthetic data is currently used for evaluation, not training, and constitutes roughly 90% of their datasets. He reports clinicians distinguished synthetic from real records about 60% of the time in blind review.
takeaways: Sample outcomes and symbolic policy paths explicitly to cover rare scenarios instead of relying on one-shot LLM diversity.
Generate records in stages that mirror real patient encounters, avoiding context overload and inconsistent long documents.
Validate cross-document consistency and round-trip agreement with the originally sampled outcome.
Give domain experts control of generation, evaluation, and pipeline skills so cases reflect realistic clinical failure modes.
reason: Included because it provides a concrete methodology for constructing, validating, and expert-steering synthetic evaluation datasets under strict data-retention constraints.
focus: Synthetic evaluation datasets and domain-expert validation

title: Act, Confirm, or Stop? Smarter behavior for AI assistants, wearables & robots — Amit Desai, Roku
summary: Amit Desai demonstrates how to improve voice-assistant outcomes without improving recognition accuracy. In a simplified music-request example, he assigns different user recovery costs to wrong actions, refusals and confirmations, then optimizes confidence thresholds against their combined cost. This Outcome User Cost Heuristic, or OUCH, exposes why an intuitive threshold can be inferior to a data-driven one. Adding a confirmation region changes the decision policy while leaving the underlying model unchanged. He extends the reasoning to televisions and embodied assistants, where interface modality and action consequences alter the cost model. The talk advocates evaluating user harm and recovery effort rather than accuracy in isolation.
takeaways: Weight failure types by their actual user consequences.
Optimize act, confirm and abstain policies using labeled outcomes.
Recalibrate cost assumptions when the interface or action stakes change.
reason: Central method is explicit outcome scoring and evaluation under uncertainty.

title: The unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for agentic search — Jo Kristian Bergum, Hornet.dev
summary: Jo Kristian Bergum argues that search evaluation must change when the searcher is an agent capable of reformulating many queries. Using BrowseComp-Plus, he contrasts high accuracy when evidence is supplied directly with lower end-to-end accuracy through a search tool, isolating retrieval and harness limitations from reasoning. He warns that an inadequately configured BM25 baseline can make competing methods appear stronger than they are; parameter and implementation choices matter. Rather than judge a single ranked list alone, he recommends measuring whether the complete agent reaches the correct answer. The talk also discusses query trajectories and filesystem workspaces as practical retrieval interfaces.
takeaways: Evaluate completed agent tasks, not only one-shot ranked-list relevance.
Use evidence-in-context comparisons to diagnose retrieval versus reasoning failures.
Tune and document baseline parameters before making method comparisons.
reason: Explicit agentic search evaluation critique, benchmark diagnostics and baseline validity.
focus: Agentic search evaluation and baseline validity

title: The Loop Is the Product — Roland Gavrilescu, Introspection
summary: Roland Gavrilescu argues that agent products improve through nested loops: workers generate traces and outcomes, while a second loop turns recurring failures into judges, evaluations, skills and harness changes. He proposes portable, versioned agent recipes that preserve this accumulated judgment independently of a model provider. A recruiting example shows how trace analysis reveals undesirable targeting, humans calibrate a judge, and agents generate candidate changes. Offline evaluations are necessary but insufficient: production experiments must establish that users value the creator’s preferences before a recipe is promoted. His proposed optimization target is valuable work relative to its resource cost, not raw token consumption.
takeaways: Turn recurring failure patterns into explicit judges and regression evaluations.
Use humans to calibrate judgment, then validate proposed changes with production users.
Version evaluation artifacts together with the harness and skills.
reason: Substantial treatment of judge calibration, trace-derived evals and online validation.

title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
summary: Klingen outlines an emerging open-source stack linking production traces, feedback, evaluation datasets, and automated improvement experiments. Agents can increasingly propose implementation fixes and maintain evaluation assets, but humans should approve changes that redefine optimization targets to avoid irrelevant failure chasing and overfitting. A changelog-writing demo uses human approval and edit signals to identify internal jargon and unclear customer language. Updated datasets compare a baseline and candidate, showing improved user-facing language without degrading format or accuracy in the example. Automatic release is acceptable there because the writer only opens reviewable pull requests. He also emphasizes scalable, retained trace data as agent-driven analysis becomes increasingly read-intensive.
takeaways: Keep humans responsible for datasets, criteria, and optimization direction.
Compare candidates on both target improvements and regression dimensions.
Use production feedback to drive repeatable, bounded improvement loops.
reason: Substantial treatment of online and offline evaluation loops. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
summary: Weco AI demonstrates autoresearch as a loop that proposes code changes, evaluates them, keeps improvements, and discards worse attempts. Mini Parameter Golf supplies a small training task, a fixed command, and a scalar validation objective; a dashboard records code and scores in an experiment tree. The presenters emphasize fast, stable measurements, correct optimization direction, bounded runtime, useful initial guidance, and protecting the evaluator from reward hacking. A second exercise optimizes a Flappy Bird controller across several conditions, with a hidden validation set and restricted editable code. Human steering can explore promising branches, but meaningful progress depends on the quality and integrity of the evaluation signal.
takeaways: Use fast, low-noise evaluators with explicit objectives and budgets.
Protect scoring code and keep hidden validation cases.
Inspect experiment trees and steer search rather than trust the best visible score.
reason: Core: fixed evaluation commands, validation objectives, reward hacking, and hidden-test design in autoresearch.

title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef
summary: Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender combine data-context architecture with a substantial evaluation workshop. Their comparisons hold model and task fixed while varying graph versus filesystem tools, using repeated runs, source-checked gold answers, deterministic citation checks, token counts, and tool-adoption traces. Callender distinguishes occasional success from correctness across every run, reporting stronger consistency and lower token use for the graph approach in a cached experiment. He also describes misleading early results caused by broken file paths, and repository-history leakage in bug-fixing evaluations. The presenters recommend hardening scorers and harnesses, reading traces, and pinning corpus snapshots; reported gains remain specific to their tasks and setup.
takeaways: Measure repeat-run consistency as well as whether any attempt succeeds.
Validate gold answers against source and unit-test deterministic scorers.
Inspect traces for broken tools and measure actual adoption, not just tool availability.
Prevent repository-history leakage and pin benchmark corpus snapshots.
reason: Extensive evaluation methods: repeated same-model graph/filesystem experiments, deterministic scorers, source-checked gold, consistency and token metrics, tool-adoption traces, scorer bugs, and repository-history leakage controls.

title: 1,000 Agent Tasks in a Sandbox: What Breaks When LLMs Run Code — Kevin Orellana, AWS
summary: Kevin Orellana uses coding agents to test the infrastructure those agents themselves depend on. An MCP wrapper exposes AgentCore’s code sandbox and browser, and agents generate and execute one thousand workflows across ten domains, logging results in SQLite for concurrent analysis. Failures include incorrect image encoding, null-byte handling, unreadable files, and browser memory exhaustion. He separates interface-layer defects from sandbox limits involving permissions, memory, process creation, seccomp, and eBPF. The talk also considers the limitations of model-generated tests and benchmark exploits. His recommendation is broad remote workflow fuzzing alongside local tests, because infrastructure failures can masquerade as weak agent reasoning or prevent an otherwise capable agent from completing its task.
takeaways: Test the environment through the same interfaces agents use.
Store structured results and classify interface versus sandbox failures.
Include remote limits and resource exhaustion in benchmark interpretation.
reason: Core: systematic workflow fuzzing and failure analysis of agent test environments.

title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
summary: Druid AI critiques containment rate as a misleading proxy for agent success. An agent escalating fewer conversations may look better while missing customers who actually need human attention. The presenters propose a seven-pillar scorecard covering configuration, runtime behavior, and governance, with twenty-six components scored by whether they are absent, defined, or actively governed. Business-weighted checks include mandate, permissions, budget, risk, compliance, observability, hallucination, tone, and validated outcomes. Repeated measurement against a human baseline can expose degradation hidden behind an unchanged green dashboard. The framework emphasizes matching metrics to a specific business role and industry; its composite score is a proposed management instrument, not an independently established universal benchmark.
takeaways: Choose outcome measures that reflect the agent’s actual mandate.
Re-evaluate on live traffic against human baselines.
Inspect drift across component metrics instead of trusting containment alone.
reason: Core: agent scorecard design, metric validity, human baselines, and drift evaluation.

title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
summary: Hrishi Olickel presents just-in-time ontologies as transformations built around a specific decision rather than a universal schema. The evaluation lessons come from data-work examples: ambiguous entity definitions, costly checking, and a pipeline that removed negative signs and turned a much smaller net balance into millions of debt while multiple models agreed. He separates designers, task workers, and optimizers, and recommends held-out cases, bounded pilot runs, versioned work segments, and explicit failure conditions. Cross-model disagreement can concentrate human review, but consensus can preserve shared mistaken assumptions. Cost, speed, and accuracy optimization only becomes meaningful when the execution surface, baseline, and evidence are stable enough to compare.
takeaways: Test definitions and silent transformations, not just output plausibility.
Use held-out cases and independently checked pilot baselines.
Treat cross-model agreement as a review aid, not proof of correctness.
reason: Core: data-quality error analysis, held-out tests, disagreement checks, and bounded optimization.

title: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Any Good: Evals With Phoenix & Claude — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Laurie Voss builds an evaluation loop around a Claude-powered financial analyst, beginning with Phoenix tracing and manual error analysis. A report claiming 116% analyst agreement illustrates why plausible final prose is insufficient. Code checks cover deterministic properties; model judges assess faithfulness and actionability. A generic correctness judge fails partly because it lacks fresh evidence, so she supplies research context and creates a focused custom judge. Human labels, rubric disagreements, and development/test separation help calibrate it. Repeated prompt experiments improve actionability without fixing all faithfulness failures, and a model upgrade introduces conservatism. The workshop ends with CI acceptance criteria and ongoing production sampling, emphasizing complementary measures rather than one score.
takeaways: Give each judge the evidence required to answer its specific question.
Calibrate with careful human labels and inspect disagreements.
Track tradeoffs across quality dimensions and retain regression checks in CI.
reason: Core: complete hands-on tracing, error analysis, judge calibration, experiments, and CI workflow.

title: Evals for High-Stakes AI Agents — Doneyli De Jesus & Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
summary: Annabell Schäfer and Doneyli De Jesus walk through a Langfuse evaluation loop for a fictional banking assistant. Tracing captures intermediate work, with PII masking before persistence; production samples and imported cases become datasets. Domain experts annotate outputs, comments are grouped into failure modes, and focused code checks or LLM judges score experiments. The session demonstrates prompt-change evaluation in CI and dashboards linking quality findings to operational concerns. Judge calibration against representative human labels is essential, particularly in regulated applications. A demonstrated score gate illustrates the intended workflow, but its effectiveness depends on testing candidates before promotion and connecting the gate correctly to deployment rather than merely displaying pass/fail results.
takeaways: Use expert comments to define application-specific failure modes.
Combine deterministic checks with human-calibrated judges.
Connect CI evaluation thresholds to the actual release boundary.
reason: Core: high-stakes evaluation workshop spanning traces, annotation, datasets, judges, experiments, and CI.

title: Teach Your Agent to Prove It's Done — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
summary: Nick Nisi and Zack Proser demonstrate how coding agents can produce checkable evidence instead of merely announce that a task is finished. The Midnight Snack Club application combines explicit goals, CLI health checks, browser observations, deterministic tests, and model judges. Failures feed the next repair attempt, while independent evidence includes screenshots, smoke tests, and persisted application state. The live discussion exposes limitations: a judge may miss a successful interaction, and a saved receipt may refer to code that has since changed. They advocate a stable evaluation baseline that multiple implementations can target, with checks tied to the current artifact and real user journeys rather than a passing build alone.
takeaways: Define completion in terms the agent can actually test.
Verify running user flows and persistence, not just compilation.
Invalidate old proof when the code or environment changes.
reason: Core: application eval baselines, deterministic verification, LLM judges, and current-artifact evidence.

title: What Agents Want — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse
summary: The OpenProse team proposes expressing multi-agent work as declarative contracts in Markdown rather than prescribing every implementation step. Demos include event-triggered jobs, a deliberately critical PR reviewer, and bank model documentation. Evaluation is embedded in the contract: describe the desired end state, compare runs against that specification, and preserve successful trajectories as reusable workflows. The presenters discuss development versus production behavior, historical-result comparisons, composable contracts, and differences from DSPy. The approach shifts effort toward stating what success means, but it does not remove the need for a trustworthy checker or good examples. The session presents workflow mechanics rather than independently measured reliability gains.
takeaways: Write outcome contracts that can be checked independently of execution.
Benchmark recurring runs against the same requirements.
Preserve successful trajectories without confusing one success with general reliability.
reason: Core: outcome contracts, run-level verification, and benchmarking declarative agent workflows.

title: Backtest Your Agent Against Yesterday's Web — Ryan Ahern, Exa
summary: Ryan Ahern leads a workshop using historical search to backtest agent-generated predictions. Exa Snapshot supports retrieval of known URLs and broader searches at a chosen cutoff, preventing an acquisition predictor from simply finding the later acquisition announcement. Participants propose company-acquisition features and test them at one, seven, and thirty days before the event, with comparison dates for non-acquired companies. The scoring setup and visible company list encourage rapid tuning, which also exposes overfitting. Ahern explicitly notes that a held-out set is necessary: historical cutoffs prevent future-information leakage, while unseen cases answer a separate question about generalization. The exercise demonstrates evaluation design, not validated investing performance.
takeaways: Freeze the information cutoff before the predicted event.
Inspect how the scoring rule rewards false positives and misses.
Use unseen cases as well as historical retrieval to prevent overfitting.
reason: Core: hands-on backtesting of agents with historical web inputs and holdout design.

title: How to Know When an AI Agent Can Work Unsupervised — Evan Kormos, Coinbase
summary: Evan Kormos models regulated business processes as directed workflows whose individual nodes can contain agentic loops. More iterations only help when the loop has a reliable check, and faster nodes can merely move a bottleneck elsewhere. He proposes representative evaluation datasets, domain-defined quality criteria, traces, and operational measures as a confidence mechanism for nondeterministic systems. Agents progress from fully supervised work to sampled human review and eventually exception-focused oversight when policy thresholds and measured evidence permit it. Decisions about authority remain distinct from technical capability. The emphasis is an incremental, observable transition rather than treating one successful demonstration as proof that an agent can safely work unsupervised.
takeaways: Define checks and representative datasets before increasing autonomy.
Measure the whole workflow for new bottlenecks.
Advance from supervision to sampling only against explicit policy thresholds.
reason: Core: evaluation evidence and monitoring used to determine appropriate agent autonomy.

title: The Model Swap Workshop: GPT-5.5 vs Kimi vs DeepSeek vs Mistral — Pamela Fox, Microsoft
summary: Pamela Fox compares GPT-5.5, Kimi, DeepSeek, and Mistral on shared application scenarios rather than trust general leaderboards. Examples cover letter counting, source-grounded RAG, images, language changes, tool arguments, calculation loops, and a travel agent’s use of parallel tools. The demonstrations expose different failure modes and show that prompt changes can repair some gaps but not establish universal capability. She then introduces bulk deterministic checks, human-calibrated LLM judges, ASSERT-generated rubrics and cases from a specification, and DSPy/GEPA prompt optimization. Evaluation must inspect completion, grounding, tool use, cost, and latency. Workshop comparisons are illustrative runs, not statistically definitive rankings of the models.
takeaways: Evaluate the actual scenario, language, and modality.
Check tool arguments, workflow completion, and efficiency alongside final answers.
Bootstrap custom cases, then calibrate judges and automate repeated evaluation.
reason: Core: model-swap workshop centered on application tests, judges, generated eval suites, and prompt optimization.

title: Do Not Let Models Invent Numbers - Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
summary: Vinoo Ganesh presents a finance architecture that prevents models from freely inventing numerical claims. Retrieved facts enter a citation registry with values, units, scales, periods, and provenance; deterministic code performs calculations, while models refer to registered facts. A post-processing filter removes unsupported figures, including numbers recalled from model training rather than retrieved evidence. He describes hybrid retrieval, reranking, tenant isolation, and disagreements between legitimate sources. Evaluation examples show many rejected citations and thousands of incorrect numbers from ordinary model or RAG outputs. The assurance is deliberately bounded: numerical traceability improves verification, but it does not establish that every qualitative conclusion or investment interpretation is correct.
takeaways: Represent financial facts with units, periods, and source provenance.
Keep calculations deterministic and reject unregistered numbers.
Distinguish verifiable numerical grounding from correctness of the broader narrative.
reason: Core: explicit numerical-output verification and failure analysis of financial RAG.

title: How to Write Your First AI Eval - SallyAnn DeLucia, Arize AI
summary: SallyAnn DeLucia leads a hands-on workshop on translating vague impressions into a first useful evaluator. A travel agent’s traces provide evidence about model decisions and tool calls; participants identify one quality dimension, define concrete pass and fail conditions, create a small dataset, and test an LLM judge in a prompt playground. She distinguishes traces, aggregate metrics, and evaluations, and surveys code checks, human annotations, decision models, and agent-as-judge approaches. The recommendation is to start with roughly twenty traces and one focused judge, inspect explanations, iterate on the rubric, and then align with human labels and expand toward online monitoring rather than begin with an all-purpose score.
takeaways: Read traces before deciding what to evaluate.
Judge one quality at a time with explicit pass/fail criteria.
Inspect explanations and calibrate against human judgments before scaling.
reason: Core: practical first-eval workshop covering trace analysis, rubrics, datasets, and judges.

title: Context Is the New Code — Patrick Debois, Tessl
summary: Patrick Debois proposes a Context Development Lifecycle: generate, evaluate, distribute, and observe the instructions, documentation, and skills that shape coding agents. Evaluation progresses from format linting and clarity checks to judging generated code against company rules and running tool-enabled judges against live endpoints in sandboxes. He recommends repeated trials and risk-sensitive error budgets because a single passing run is unreliable. Observation closes the loop through agent logs, pull-request feedback, and production failures converted into regression tests and improved shared context. Security discussion covers provenance, scanning, tracing, and context filtering. Q&A stresses that constructing useful, business-specific evals remains substantial engineering work rather than disappearing with prompt-based development.
takeaways: Test changes to agent instructions as behavioral changes, using layered checks from format validation to executable end-to-end scenarios.
Give judges tools when correctness requires running the generated system rather than merely inspecting its source.
Use repeated trials and risk-sensitive error budgets rather than treating one nondeterministic eval run as a reliable CI gate.
Turn recurring agent-log gaps, PR feedback, and production failures into shared context improvements and regression cases.
reason: Evaluation and quality-linked observability are explicit, substantial lifecycle stages. The transcript explains concrete context tests, LLM and tool-enabled judging, repeated nondeterministic trials, error budgets, and production-to-regression feedback. The Q&A also addresses the effort required to construct business-specific evals, making this a direct core inclusion.
focus: Context evaluation, tool-enabled judges, and quality observability

title: Ship Real Agents: Hands-On Evals for Agentic Applications — Laurie Voss, Arize
summary: Voss builds an evaluation workflow around a two-stage financial-analysis agent, using Phoenix tracing to inspect tool calls, diagnose failures, and prioritize fixes. He combines deterministic checks, built-in LLM judges, and a custom actionability rubric with concrete examples. A correctness judge rejects current financial data because it lacks temporal context, whereas a source-grounded faithfulness judge passes the same runs, demonstrating that evaluator selection changes the signal. Meta-evaluation covers human labels, held-out examples, precision, recall, and judge biases, although the workshop's human annotations are explicitly randomized demonstration data. Experiments compare prompt revisions on failures; Q&A recommends periodically rerunning the full corpus to detect overfitting and regressions.
takeaways: Read traces before writing evaluators, distinguish symptoms from root causes, and prioritize observed failures by frequency and severity.
Use deterministic checks for objective constraints and LLM judges for semantic requirements; faithfulness to supplied research does not establish independent factual correctness.
Calibrate focused rubrics with genuine human-labeled examples and held-out data, inspect disagreements and biases, and do not treat the randomized workshop labels as validation.
Compare prompt versions with fixed inputs and evaluators, repeat trials for nondeterminism, and periodically run the full evaluation corpus to catch regressions beyond targeted failures.
reason: This is an end-to-end evaluation workshop covering instrumentation, trace-based error analysis, deterministic tests, built-in and custom judges, meta-evaluation, datasets, experiments, reliability measures, and regression testing. Phoenix setup and financial-agent scaffolding support those methods rather than replacing them with a general platform presentation.

title: The maturity phases of running evals — Phil Hetzel, Braintrust
summary: Phil Hetzel outlines a progression from documented human review to scalable, production-informed agent evaluation. Early reviewers should record both a quality judgment and the reasoning behind it, allowing teams to derive specific failure modes and create deterministic scorers or LLM judges. Judges themselves need validation against trusted human labels. As agents use external systems, evaluation expands from final outputs to full traces, with special attention to reconstructing historical state and avoiding destructive production writes during replay. The talk favors focused failure coverage over impossible exhaustive testing and identifies automated topic modeling and agent-driven workflows as emerging practices.
takeaways: Capture expert rationales, not just binary annotations.
Evaluate the evaluator before scaling LLM-as-judge scoring.
Represent historical external-system state and isolate side effects in offline evaluation.
reason: Dedicated evaluation maturity, full-trace testing and judge calibration.

title: LLM Observability, Evaluation, Experimentation Platform — Dat Ngo, Arize
summary: Dat Ngo demonstrates how observability, evaluation and experimentation fit together in Arize’s tooling. OpenTelemetry traces expose tool calls and branches, while sessions and distributional views reveal failures beyond one run. Evaluation signals include expert gold sets, end-user feedback, deterministic checks and LLM judges calibrated against trusted annotations. He distinguishes span, multi-span, trajectory and session-level assessments, advising teams to choose the smallest useful set rather than evaluate everything. Production traces become datasets for comparing prompt, model and orchestration changes. The presentation also shows agent-accessible tools intended to automate failure discovery and the improvement loop.
takeaways: Choose evaluation scope to match the question: component, trajectory or full session.
Calibrate judges against domain-expert annotations.
Convert trace failures into controlled experiments and monitor regressions.
reason: Dedicated observability/evaluation/experimentation platform explanation and demo.
focus: Observability, judge calibration and experiment scopes

title: Stop Making Models Bigger, Make Them Behave — Kobie Crawford, Snorkel
summary: Kobie Crawford presents a financial-analysis study where targeted reinforcement learning improves a small model’s tool discipline more than selecting a much larger reasoning model. A self-contained FinQA environment supplies verifiable answers and separate single-table and harder multi-table benchmarks. Trace comparisons show the larger model guessing table names and hallucinating after failed queries, while the trained model discovers schemas and corrects errors. Single-table training generalizes to multi-table evaluation. The practical evaluation lesson is to decompose correctness into behavioral rubrics, identify the failing component, and generate training data for that behavior instead of interpreting a final-answer score as a diagnosis.
takeaways: Inspect tool trajectories to distinguish reasoning gaps from tool-discipline failures.
Use component rubrics to choose what training data to create.
Test transfer on harder held-out task types rather than only trained scenarios.
reason: Substantial benchmark design, trajectory diagnosis and rubric-driven improvement.

title: The Miranda Hypothesis: How Hamilton Poisoned Persona Evals - Jacob E. Thomas, Results Gen
summary: Jacob E. Thomas argues that fluent, personality-consistent historical personas can still reason from anachronistic cultural composites. Hamilton and Lincoln demonstrations illustrate why convincingness is not documentary fidelity. His proposed Prism experiment compares primary-source, biography and bare-model conditions at distinct moments in Lincoln’s life using historian-authored diagnostic questions. A preregistered rubric weights anachronism, documentary consistency and contextual plausibility, deliberately excluding rhetorical polish as an independent reward. The talk is explicit that large-scale results are not yet available. Domain experts design gold sets and adjudicate edge cases at build and release gates rather than reviewing every runtime conversation.
takeaways: Validate whether your rubric measures the actual failure mode rather than fluency.
Use temporally bounded sources and domain-expert gold sets for persona fidelity.
Separate observed examples from preregistered predictions and future findings.
reason: Entire talk addresses evaluation construct validity, experimental design and expert adjudication.

title: How we taught agents to use good retrieval - Hanna Lichtenberg, Mixedbread AI
summary: Mixedbread explains an oracle gap: models answer difficult knowledge questions better when supplied the right documents than when they must retrieve them. BrowseComp+ and OfficeQA Pro illustrate the gap and the limitations of keyword-shaped benchmark queries. The speakers build a bounded, parallel search harness with semantic search, metadata filtering and grep, then train a smaller agent using supervised examples and on-policy reinforcement learning. Rewards combine retrieval metrics with LLM rubrics for relevance, ranking, query formulation and exploration. Preliminary results distinguish the unreleased trained system from an existing production search offering, emphasizing evaluation of retrieval behavior rather than reasoning alone.
takeaways: Measure retrieval against an oracle-document baseline to localize failure.
Use separate relevance, ranking and trajectory rubrics rather than one final-answer score.
Match keyword and semantic tools to different evidence needs.
reason: Benchmark bias, retrieval evaluation and LLM reward rubrics are substantial topics.

title: Build Evals That Actually Matter - Nick Ung & Akshay Sharma, Lyft
summary: Nick Ung and Akshay Sharma describe Lyft’s end-to-end customer-support evaluation lifecycle. Offline multi-turn simulations combine representative tasks, personas, deterministic checks, and LLM judges before launch; production traces and expert annotation then drive continuing error analysis. Helpful frontier models made unrealistically polite simulated customers, inflating results, so Lyft fine-tuned a user simulator on real verbatim conversations. Judges are treated as classifiers with specific binary business rubrics, human labels, held-out validation, and precision/recall measurement. The speakers emphasize criteria drift, confidence intervals, sufficient samples, accountable regression owners, and scores that actually gate decisions. A standardized, config-driven harness is presented as continuing work rather than a fully completed system.
takeaways: Make simulated users resemble real difficult conversations, not helpful assistants.
Validate each judge against human labels and task-specific binary criteria.
Require decision-relevant launch gates, uncertainty estimates, and regression ownership.
reason: Direct end-to-end eval lifecycle, realistic user simulations, judge validation, and statistical rigor.

title: The Future of Evals: From LLM as a Judge to Agent as a Judge — Aparna Dhinakaran, Arize AI
summary: Aparna Dhinakaran argues that evaluation must evolve with agents: fixed prompt-response checks no longer cover systems with memory, dynamic interfaces, repeated tools, subagents, and long-running trajectories. Drawing on Arize’s production experience, she distinguishes deterministic checks, conventional rubric-based LLM judges, and adaptive agent-as-judge analysis. The third approach investigates traces to discover failures that were not anticipated in a predefined rubric, such as inefficient repeated tool calls or completion and context-management problems. She introduces Signal as a long-running investigator that groups issues and can propose fixes. Her recommendation is additive rather than replacement: use all three evaluation styles for their respective strengths.
takeaways: Retain deterministic checks and rubric-based judges while adding adaptive investigation.
Look beyond final answers to trajectory-level failures and inefficient loops.
Use newly discovered production issues to fuel continual improvement.
reason: Direct conceptual treatment of deterministic, LLM-as-judge, and agent-as-judge evaluation.

title: Evaling Video Slop — Maor Bril, Character.ai
summary: Maor Bril describes why generated-video evaluation must capture storytelling, physical plausibility, pacing, identity consistency, and audio synchronization rather than individual-frame similarity alone. Character.ai combined conventional metrics with human-calibrated model judges, then distilled that expensive process into a small vision-language model for faster feedback during generation. Pairwise comparisons proved more useful than absolute scores. Early versions confidently rewarded visual polish rather than the intended quality axes, requiring better training pairs and consistent encoding and annotation to avoid learning an AI-versus-human detector. Bril emphasizes detecting errors before full videos are assembled, continually recalibrating against human judgments, and choosing judge size according to latency and unit economics.
takeaways: Use pairwise preferences and explicit quality axes instead of vague absolute scores.
Audit training pairs for shortcuts such as production-source or encoding artifacts.
Place quality checks early inside generation and recalibrate with human feedback.
reason: Direct multimodal evaluation, judge calibration, pairwise preferences, and failure analysis.

title: Ending AI Slop — Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs
summary: Castello Branco argues that improving design and writing requires decomposing subjective quality rather than treating taste as one undifferentiated score. Brand adherence illustrates the method: extract colors, typography, spacing, motion, and other constraints, then judge new work against those properties instead of copying a reference. More verifiable components can support reinforcement-learning environments, while creativity and contextual style fit require expert human judgment. She warns that pooling incompatible preferences produces bland averages and recommends preserving audience, style, and temporal context. Her data-quality framework stresses carefully selected experts, specific explanations grounded in visible or code components, and QA that distinguishes objective errors from legitimate aesthetic disagreement.
takeaways: Break subjective goals into observable components and choose evaluation methods per component rather than asking one judge whether an artifact is simply good.
Grade brand-consistent novelty against explicit design constraints, not resemblance to a single reference output.
Preserve differing human preferences with contextual information; disagreement about aesthetics is not automatically annotation noise.
Improve feedback specificity by connecting expert comments to exact visual or code components, while reserving consensus checks for properties experts should objectively agree on.
reason: Develops concrete approaches to subjective judging, component-level verification, preference preservation, and evaluation-data quality assurance.

title: Rethinking Environments for Long-Horizon Work — Rayan Garg, Theta Software
summary: Theta's presenters argue that long-horizon capability cannot be captured by human task duration alone: token consumption, tool coordination, sequential state dependencies, and ambiguity reveal different difficulties. They distinguish genuinely dependent workflows from artificially concatenated tasks and explain why open-ended work complicates standardized grading. Their proposed judges act as agents, inspecting final environment state through safeguarded read-only tools and querying structured trajectories rather than receiving one oversized transcript. They discuss combining deterministic checks with rubric judging, partial credit, reward-density tradeoffs, and quality tests for gold solutions, no-ops, variance, coverage, and expert agreement. The closing critique questions existing finance benchmarks' horizon claims, domain breadth, saturation, and usefulness as learning signals.
takeaways: Report both human-time and model-execution measures, with harness and task methodology held explicit; neither alone establishes long-horizon difficulty.
Build tasks with consequential state changes and dependencies rather than merely chaining independent subtasks to inflate length.
Give judges read-only access to relevant system state and searchable trajectories so they can verify outcomes without mutating the evaluated environment.
Quality-test rubrics against gold and no-op solutions, judge variance, coverage, and expert agreement before using their rewards for training or comparisons.
reason: Substantively develops long-horizon measurement methodology, environment-aware judging, rubric validation, and benchmark error analysis.
focus: Long-horizon agent evaluation and agentic judges

title: Shipping AI to a Million Patients Without an A/B Test — Jared Joselowitz, Ufonia
summary: Jared Joselowitz explains Ufonia's safety-evaluation stack for DORA, arguing that irreversible clinical conversations require evidence before patient exposure. He describes around 200,000 completed UK calls and contracts to reach a million patients. Matrix simulates clinical scenarios with Patbot patients and uses an automated judge to identify hazards against clinician-defined behaviors. Both patient realism and judge accuracy are validated; he reports a judge F1 of 0.96 on a clinician-labeled corpus. Automated prompt optimization uses harm-sensitive objectives rather than flat accuracy. Simulation then feeds staged user testing, supervised clinical evaluation, and monitored deployment. He stresses that simulation is necessary but insufficient, and that prompts, verdicts, and datasets must trace to specific hazards.
takeaways: Derive test scenarios from product-specific harms and deliberately manufacture rare, dangerous edge cases.
Validate both simulated-patient behavior and automated judges against human evidence before trusting large-scale simulation scores.
Use harm-sensitive cost functions, prioritizing red-flag sensitivity when missed hazards are more costly than false alarms.
Require staged clinical evidence after simulation and preserve hazard-linked prompts, datasets, traces, and judge verdicts.
reason: Included because it details hazard-derived testing, simulator and judge validation, harm-weighted optimization, and evidence-based release gates for clinical agents.
focus: Hazard-based simulation, judge validation, and clinical release gates

title: Inside 847 Production Clinical AI Notes — Sebastian Fox, Composo
summary: Sebastian Fox examines dangerous failures in clinical notes that remain fluent and superficially faithful: omitted red flags, inferred symptoms, and plans preserved after clinicians abandoned them. He distinguishes transcription mistakes from generation errors and argues that spotting textual differences is easier than judging their clinical significance. In his tests, even a carefully engineered rubric-based judge approved notes containing serious errors. His proposed alternative is a continuous discover, capture, and calibrate loop: cluster failures from real outputs, collect expert reasoning and corrections, and retrieve relevant precedents and guidelines for each judgment. He reports improved detection on the same notes when the judge receives this case-specific context instead of a frozen standard.
takeaways: Audit omissions and altered clinical intent, not just obvious hallucinations or surface-level faithfulness.
Discover failure categories from real outputs rather than relying exclusively on imagined or synthetic cases.
Capture experts' explanations and corrections alongside scores so tacit contextual judgment becomes reusable evidence.
Retrieve relevant adjudicated cases and guidelines per output, updating the evaluator as standards and failure modes change.
reason: Included because the entire talk addresses production error analysis, limitations of static LLM judges, and continuous expert calibration of evaluation.
focus: Clinical error analysis and expert-calibrated LLM judges

title: AI Evals for Cross-Functional Teams — Nachiket Paranjape & Swaroop Chitlur Haridas, DoorDash
summary: DoorDash’s GenAI platform speakers describe evaluation as a shared workflow rather than an engineering-only test harness. Strategy and operations set quality priorities, product translates requirements into rubrics, operations supplies annotations, and engineering provides stable APIs, telemetry, datasets and judges. Their continuous loop captures traces, samples reviewable subsets, annotates them with domain expertise, creates golden datasets and calibrates judges before repeating. API-first infrastructure lets operators build their own annotation interfaces with coding agents. A self-service calibration UI exposes original and revised judge prompts for review. The speakers report lower annotation costs and faster iteration, but the captions provide no numeric cost-reduction figure.
takeaways: Assign domain experts meaningful ownership of quality definitions and annotations.
Make trace sampling, golden-set creation and judge calibration one continuous workflow.
Expose judge-prompt changes so non-engineers can review calibration results.
reason: Direct evaluation platform, human annotation and LLM-judge calibration talk.
focus: Cross-functional evaluation platforms and judge calibration

title: SOTA Generative Media Panel — Dumitru Erhan, Shane Gu & Nicole Brichtova, Google DeepMind
summary: This Google DeepMind panel explains why attractive generative-media outputs are not necessarily useful or faithful. A side-by-side experiment found people often preferred generated versions of real videos because they looked sharper or more saturated, illustrating weaknesses of broad preference scores. The panel contrasts automatable checks, such as OCR-based text-rendering verification, with difficult aesthetic and free-form editing judgments. Evaluation combines large human studies, live experiments, expert inspection and early-access workflow feedback. Examples include missed details, implausible eye gaze and unexpected wedding rings. Their practical message is to evaluate instruction following and real creative workflows, rather than optimizing a single generic beauty judgment.
takeaways: Separate aesthetic preference from fidelity, instruction following and workflow usefulness.
Automate objective checks where possible, but retain expert and human assessment.
Use early-access practitioners to uncover regressions hidden by aggregate preference gains.
reason: Extended discussion of video/image evaluation, human-preference artifacts, automatic-rater limits and workflow-grounded checks; not merely a launch panel.
focus: Generative-media evaluation and human preference validity

title: Training Taste — Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs
summary: Thais Castello Branco explains how Taste Labs decomposes subjective design quality into measurable characteristics. Some attributes, such as contrast or alignment in a defined context, admit broad expert agreement; others require data and acknowledgment of disagreement. Her team analyzes over two million historical websites alongside synthetic designs, mining structured features and training small classifier probes. Combined probe patterns predict repetitive, context-insensitive design, reportedly outperforming generic LLM judging, though no detailed numeric comparison is supplied in the captions. She connects measurement to intervention: deliberate creative divergence and structured brand representations give agents both guidance and criteria against which their outputs can be checked.
takeaways: Decompose subjective quality into specific observable attributes.
Distinguish expert-consensus checks from genuinely preference-dependent judgments.
Evaluate brand adherence against explicit structured references rather than generic taste.
reason: Central topic is measuring design quality, classifier-based judging and verification.

title: The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)
summary: Paul Bakaus treats skills as harness extensions rather than packaged prompts, combining independent critiques, deterministic linting, hooks and model-specific behavior. His evaluation setup recreates several agent harnesses and tools, simulates interactive users, and compares skill releases across models and design niches. Rule identifiers enable ablations: remove a line, rerun evaluations, restore it and measure effects with deterministic checks. He also explains limits of visual taste judges, including a model rewarding crowded viewports, and retains human annotation for subjective assessment. The workshop’s quality lesson is to test actual cross-harness behavior and enforce required validation steps rather than assume prose instructions guarantee compliance.
takeaways: Run cross-model and cross-harness tests rather than validating only the author’s setup.
Ablate individual skill rules to establish whether they improve measured behavior.
Keep independent critiques and human judgment when design judges reward spurious features.
reason: Substantial eval harness, line ablations, judge failure analysis and validation mechanisms; full publisher transcript recovered after native cap.
focus: Skill evaluation, ablations and design judges

title: Modality Misalignment and Originality Attribution in Short-Form Video — Aditya Gautam, Meta
summary: Aditya Gautam describes specialized video agents for modality misalignment and originality attribution, then explains how production evaluation sustains them. A perceiver, retriever and reviewer divide temporal analysis, evidence retrieval and decision-making. Daily production samples pass through an in-house judge and human review; failures are traced to reasoning, tool calls or retrieval before preference data informs further training. Evaluation includes precision, recall and F1, but also per-node latency, reasoning budgets, robustness and token costs. Crucially, the judge itself is checked against the human queue for drift. The talk ties task quality, infrastructure efficiency and ongoing monitoring into one continuous improvement process.
takeaways: Attribute failures at agent, tool and retrieval levels instead of relying only on final accuracy.
Continuously compare automated judges with human review to detect drift.
Evaluate efficiency changes alongside task quality and reasoning-budget tradeoffs.
reason: Substantive production feedback loop, component-level evaluation and judge monitoring.
focus: Production agent evaluation and judge drift

title: Skill issue: stop deploying vision language models, use them with Skills — Merve Noyan, Hugging Face
summary: Merve Noyan presents a workflow in which a larger vision-language model labels images, smaller VLM judges inspect overlaid bounding boxes, and accepted examples train a compact detector. She evaluates road-sign outputs against ground-truth labels and explores document parsing where the trained detector sometimes catches objects missed by its labeler. The talk’s key quality lesson is judge imbalance: requiring both judges to approve would discard too much data, so her experiment accepts an example if either approves. Human review remains necessary for judge prompts and augmentation policies; agent-generated horizontal sign flips and traffic-light color jitter illustrate destructive defaults. Model choice also considers licensing and deployment speed.
takeaways: Inspect each judge’s rejection behavior before choosing an ensemble rule.
Compare pseudo-label pipelines with ground truth when available.
Review augmentation policies and judge prompts rather than trusting coding-agent defaults.
reason: Substantial VLM-as-judge methodology, annotation evaluation and error analysis.
focus: VLM annotation quality and judge ensembles
date_source: Reviewer-verified YouTube or publisher upload date

title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
summary: Kumar introduces evaluations as predeployment reliability instrumentation complementary to runtime harness safeguards. He surveys exact matching, schema validation, pairwise comparisons, and LLM judges, highlighting position, sycophancy, self-preference, and verbosity biases. A live returns-policy example progresses from brittle keyword checks to a policy-grounded judge calibrated against approximately thirty labeled examples, then a CI agreement gate. Adding missing policy context and upgrading the judge improve the demonstration; network timeouts and label formatting complicate results. He recommends version-pinned judges, continuously refreshed production examples, and shared retrievable policy for agent and judge, demonstrated through OpenRAG. His suggested agreement thresholds and perfect-agreement warning are heuristics, not guarantees of safety or generalization.
takeaways: Start with cheap deterministic checks and escalate only when needed.
Ground judges in the same current policy as production agents.
Monitor agreement and inspect disagreements instead of trusting green scores.
reason: Substantial treatment of evaluation methods and judge calibration. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Voss walks through instrumenting a financial-research agent, reading complete traces, categorizing failures, and building deterministic, built-in, and custom evaluations. A context-free correctness judge rejects current financial information, while source-grounded faithfulness exposes unsupported claims. The workshop then calibrates actionability judgments against human labels, discusses precision, recall, held-out data, bias, and focused rubrics, and converts failures into experiment datasets. Coding-agent-generated prompt revisions are compared using the same evaluations, with passing cases retained for regression checks. Some labels and failure categories are deliberately random demonstration data, and the polished improvement result is explicitly unrepresentative. Production sampling and ongoing dataset maintenance complete the proposed engineering loop.
takeaways: Read traces and define domain-specific success before writing evaluators.
Provide judges the evidence needed for the question being scored.
Calibrate judges and test fixes against both failing and passing examples.
reason: Substantial treatment of evaluation design and judge calibration. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Your LLM Judge Is a Confident Liar: Building Better Verifiers — Browserbase
summary: Browserbase and Microsoft researchers show how weak web-task judges can reward false success, citing one agent scored near seventy-four percent by an existing judge versus roughly thirty-eight percent by their verifier. Their universal verifier generates task-specific rubrics, retrieves relevant screenshot evidence per criterion, and separates partial process credit from actual outcome success and environmental blockers. Evaluation uses human annotations, held-out trajectories, agreement measures, and controlled training-data filtering experiments. They report better downstream models and strong human agreement on their collected labels, not universal infallibility. Autoresearch accelerates verifier development, but unprimed automation falls short of human-designed quality; combining human insights with automated experiments performs better.
takeaways: Verify environment evidence rather than agent claims.
Separate controllable mistakes, partial progress, and outcome completion.
Hold out human-labeled trajectories when tuning verifiers.
reason: Substantial treatment of llm judges and verifier validation. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Your Fridge Is a Valid Payment Device — Eleonora Drykina & Nina Žižakić, In The Pocket
summary: Eleonora Drykina and Nina Žižakić describe a payment-rulebook assistant whose quality depends on preserving tables, section structure, and citations across hundreds of PDFs. Their retrieval-only test on sixty-three questions raises reported hit rate from ninety-two to ninety-seven percent with hybrid search, but they distinguish this from answer correctness. Roughly eighty-six Promptfoo end-to-end cases combine rubric-based LLM judgment with source-document citation checks, informed by real user tests and behavioral rules. Repeated runs expose judge noise: five of twelve apparent flips do not reproduce, and one alleged hallucinated date is actually in the source. Traces and direct document inspection therefore remain necessary when interpreting evaluation changes.
takeaways: Evaluate retrieval and complete answers separately.
Check citation targets alongside rubric-based model judgments.
Rerun apparent regressions and challenge the rubric against source documents.
reason: Core: real-world RAG evaluation, retrieval benchmarks, citation checks, and nonreproducible judge failures.

title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
summary: Louis-François Bouchard introduces ToneBench for assessing writing that matches a particular voice rather than merely avoiding conspicuous AI vocabulary. Ten script tasks, five drafts per model, four LLM judges, and nine metrics address tone, writing quality, instruction following, research accuracy, and slop. Detailed rubrics require explanations and examples, while blind judging and one thousand human A/B comparisons help expose weaknesses. He reports that judges can prefer their own model family and that rubric or generation-prompt changes make reruns expensive. The benchmark measures one author’s preferences, not universal writing quality.
