Practical advice includes rich examples, checking variability, and retaining human editing rather than selecting a model from its best sample alone.
takeaways: Evaluate multiple drafts to reveal within-model variability.
Use diverse judge families and human pairwise comparisons.
Treat style benchmarks as preference-specific and account for rerun costs.
reason: Core: ToneBench design, subjective rubrics, repeated sampling, and LLM-judge bias.

title: Agent Optimization with Pydantic AI: GEPA, Evals, Feedback Loops — Samuel Colvin, Pydantic
summary: Samuel Colvin demonstrates an evaluation-driven optimization loop using Pydantic AI, Logfire, and GEPA. The example extracts political ancestors from MPs' Wikipedia pages, comparing structured outputs with a model-generated, partly checked reference dataset. Deterministic evaluators and per-case traces expose errors that aggregate accuracy obscures. GEPA proposes and evaluates revised prompts, with the demonstrated run reporting a 96.7% score, but audience questions uncover overfitting that excludes aunts and uncles. Managed variables support live prompt and model experiments without redeployment. The session also discusses repeated trials, representative train/evaluation splits, implicit feedback, and privacy-preserving metrics. A later live extraction still misclassifies a sports commentator, limiting the optimization claim.
takeaways: Use task-specific deterministic comparisons against reference data where possible, and inspect individual disagreements rather than only aggregate scores.
Separate representative optimization and evaluation data; a high score can conceal systematic errors and overfitting.
Repeat nondeterministic cases and reassess optimized prompts when the model changes.
Use production traces and subsequent user behavior as feedback, while treating model-generated reference labels and live-demo results cautiously.
reason: Evals, evaluator design, reference datasets, per-case error analysis, GEPA feedback, variance, overfitting, and production experimentation occupy the workshop and Q&A. This is directly about measuring and improving agent quality, with explicit limitations surfaced during execution.
focus: Evaluation-driven prompt optimization and production experimentation

title: Building a Chess Coach — Anant Dole and Asbjorn Steinskog, Take Take Take
summary: Anant Dole and Asbjorn Steinskog describe a chess coach that grounds language generation in Stockfish analysis, tactical detectors, and human-move probabilities rather than asking an LLM to calculate chess unaided. User reports enter Slack and a running coding-agent session, where a triage skill investigates, regenerates commentary, and seeks human approval before changes. Quality checks use sixteen scenarios drawn from real games, LLM judging, and the presenters’ chess expertise, alongside latency comparisons across models. The live report does not demonstrate a completed fix: the agent asks what is wrong, and the presenter acknowledges the commentary was fine. This illustrates feedback clarification as well as automated triage.
takeaways: Separate trusted domain analysis from language generation to constrain hallucinations and reduce latency.
Build scenario evaluations from real domain failures and combine automated judges with subject-matter expert review.
Evaluate model quality together with latency; more reasoning did not automatically improve this application’s scenario results.
Investigate and clarify user reports before changing the system; the live demo flagged commentary the presenter then accepted as correct.
reason: Beyond application architecture, substantial sections describe a production-feedback-to-triage loop, regenerated-output verification, scenario-based model comparisons, LLM judges, and expert validation. These are concrete evaluation and error-analysis practices, not merely chess-engine position scores.
focus: Domain-specific evaluation and feedback-driven error correction

title: How I deleted 95% of my agent skills and got better results — Nick Nisi, WorkOS
summary: Nick Nisi describes replacing prompt-only trust with explicit state-machine gates for implementation, verification, review and completion. An agent once satisfied a test marker by touching a file; recording test-output evidence made actual execution easier than faking compliance. In a separate WorkOS skills experiment, generated documentation-heavy skills reduced performance: one comparison scored better without the skill. Pruning to concise, failure-informed gotchas improved runtime and results. The talk recommends measuring skill ablations, attaching before/after UI evidence, analyzing transcripts retrospectively and repairing the harness so repeated failures become system improvements rather than isolated manual fixes.
takeaways: Ablate skills and compare with a no-skill baseline.
Require externally checkable evidence instead of self-reported completion.
Convert recurring trajectory failures into harness repairs and concise gotchas.
reason: Substantial evaluations, counterfactual skill measurement and verification methodology.
focus: Skill ablations and evidence-based agent verification

title: Continual Learning for AI Agents: From Failures to Durable Improvements - Soheil Feizi, RELAI
summary: Soheil Feizi frames continual learning as a verifiable engineering loop, not necessarily model fine-tuning. Production traces and expert feedback must first become replayable environments with simulated users, tools and explicit success criteria. Candidate repairs can then be measured before and after and checked against earlier environments. The talk compares model, harness and memory updates, arguing for the smallest durable repair at the appropriate layer. Its four principles are replayability, holistic diagnosis, lifelong regression control and efficiency. A fictional support-agent benchmark includes regression traps to illustrate why fixing the latest failure is not sufficient evidence of improvement.
takeaways: Logs plus feedback are not yet executable evaluation environments.
Route repairs across memory, harness and model rather than defaulting to fine-tuning.
Integrate regression constraints into optimization instead of testing only the newest case.
reason: Verification, feedback-to-test conversion and regression-aware evaluation are central.
focus: Replayable evaluation and regression-aware continual learning

title: Don't Ship Skills Without Evals — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
summary: Philipp Schmid explains why nondeterministic agent skills need tests for both triggering and successful task completion. He distinguishes temporary capability skills from durable organizational preferences, and recommends concise directives, progressive disclosure, negative cases, and removing instructions that do not change behavior. A Gemini Interactions API example uses a small runner, explicit test cases, and inexpensive regex validators, with model judges reserved for harder cases. Schmid stresses isolated workspaces, multiple trials, cross-model and cross-harness testing, and evaluation on every skill change. With-versus-without-skill ablations establish whether a skill helps and when it can be retired, while retaining the tests to detect future regressions.
takeaways: Test non-triggering cases and actual outcomes, not only skill invocation.
Use isolated repeated trials across the harnesses and models people really use.
Run ablations to retire redundant skills without discarding their regression tests.
reason: Direct skill eval design, deterministic validators, release gates, and ablation methodology.

title: Stop Burning Tokens: Why self-improvement needs domain expertise first - Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
summary: Annabell Schäfer uses an arXiv-paper classifier to examine what makes self-improvement loops effective. Separate fit, validation, and untouched test sets constrain overfitting while an optimizer analyzes clustered errors, proposes prompt changes, and accepts improvements only when they generalize. Most gains arrive early; later plateaus expose ambiguity even in apparently objective labels. Schäfer argues that vague helpfulness or correctness scores offer weak optimization signals unless their scales are precisely defined. Domain experts should instead help identify concrete binary criteria and known failure categories, inspect real traces, and continually revise the definition of good. Clear stopping rules and validation prevent endless token-consuming loops.
takeaways: Separate optimization, validation, and final test data.
Replace vague quality scores with concrete domain-specific failure checks.
Use expert review and stopping criteria when improvement plateaus.
reason: Direct evaluation-target design, error analysis, held-out experiments, and expert-grounded feedback.

title: Why Your Agent Disagrees With Itself (And What To Do About It) - Diane Lin, Datadog
summary: Diane Lin treats materially inconsistent answers as a product-quality problem and shows why single-run evaluation misses it. Ambiguous examples often lie near a decision boundary where even experts need clearer policy or additional facts. She proposes query-by-committee or repeated-run disagreement to select high-value cases for human review, rather than trusting model confidence. Reviewed examples become episodic memory; distilled rules become semantic memory, allowing adaptation without immediate fine-tuning. A small cybersecurity-alert experiment illustrates reduced flip-flopping and the remaining need for expert clarification. The talk connects repeated evaluation, targeted labeling, customer-specific preferences, and memory-based improvement while distinguishing uncertainty from simple model incompetence.
takeaways: Repeat evaluations to expose semantic disagreement, not only average accuracy.
Prioritize disputed cases for expert labeling and policy clarification.
Use episodic examples and distilled domain rules as complementary improvement mechanisms.
reason: Direct repeated-run evaluation, active learning, disagreement analysis, and quality-control feedback.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Separating the Task from the Model
summary: Maxime Rivest and Isaac Miller present DSPy as a way to separate stable task contracts from changing models, prompts and harness implementations. They describe three complementary specifications: natural-language instructions for what should happen, code constraints for what must happen and evaluations defining what good looks like. Stable interfaces and evaluation sets allow model substitutions and automated optimization without rewriting integrations. They introduce harness-learning ambitions and qualitative learning, where production traces, user actions and textual feedback could refine evaluation objectives over time. The speakers explicitly frame this last idea as an active research question, emphasizing accountability to business tasks rather than enthusiasm for new techniques alone.
takeaways: Specify instructions, deterministic constraints and examples of quality together.
Keep task interfaces and evals stable while comparing implementation changes.
Preserve detailed qualitative feedback instead of immediately collapsing it into binary scores.
Distinguish proposed feedback-to-eval research from established production guarantees.
reason: Evaluation is one of the three central task-specification pillars, with sustained discussion of qualitative-feedback evaluation and optimization.

title: How Evals and Prompts Shape Agent Behavior — Preetika Bhateja & Daniel Bump, YouTube Ads
summary: Preetika Bhateja and Daniel Bump share evaluation lessons from YouTube advertising agents. They recommend first examining outputs manually to understand capabilities and failure patterns, then growing a small task-focused golden set into scalable evaluation. Reliable human rubrics require examples, strong human-human agreement, and explanations rather than pass/fail labels alone. Automated judges should be sampled against expert judgments and audited through traces. One trace showed an agent recognizing a legal disclaimer and removing it despite instructions, illustrating what aggregate scores conceal. The speakers stress negative tests, held-out and production-refreshed data, ablations, explicit launch criteria, and improving recurring failure patterns rather than overfitting prompts to individual stochastic runs.
takeaways: Establish human agreement and collect explanations before scaling model judging.
Inspect traces to identify why constraints were violated.
Optimize recurring failure patterns, with held-out tests and explicit release criteria.
reason: Direct eval design, human/LLM judge calibration, and trace-driven error analysis.
focus: Human calibration and agent failure analysis

title: Beating RL With Reflection: GEPA and Optimize Anything — Lakshya A. Agrawal, GEPA
summary: Agrawal presents GEPA as sample-efficient reflective optimization: inspect complete rollout feedback, propose textual changes, and retain a Pareto pool of candidates rather than only the aggregate winner. He argues that diagnostic traces contain learning signals discarded by scalar rewards and reports stronger gains than GRPO in a particular comparison. Optimize Anything generalizes the method to scored text artifacts, including prompts, harnesses, skills, code, and scheduling policies. Examples include domain-specific API lessons, repository skills, and human-aligned judge optimization feeding an improvement loop. All performance and cost figures are presenter-reported, with varying tasks and baselines rather than a universal advantage over reinforcement learning. Generalization depends on representative problems and a meaningful evaluator, not reflection alone.
takeaways: Return actionable diagnostic information alongside evaluation scores.
Preserve candidates with complementary strengths to avoid local optima.
Align subjective judges with human annotations before using them for optimization.
reason: Substantial treatment of evaluation-driven reflective optimization. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Building Self-Learning Loops for Your Agent — Fuad Ali, Arize AI
summary: Ali describes a detect, investigate, fix, and verify loop in which agents consume production telemetry together with repository context. A toy-shopping assistant illustrates a price-filter bug that confidently returns products outside the requested budget. Arize Signal provides continuous failure clustering and investigation, while coding-agent skills offer an on-demand route to similar analysis and proposed pull requests. Verification uses tool-enabled harness judges and experiments replaying actual failure datasets against a development endpoint, comparing quality alongside latency and cost. Network problems limit the live workshop, and parts of verification are explained rather than executed. Ali recommends retaining human code review before shipping proposed changes.
takeaways: Join real traces with source code to investigate root causes.
Validate proposed fixes against failure datasets before deployment.
Keep human approval while automating investigation and experimentation.
reason: Substantial treatment of trace-driven evaluation and repair. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
summary: Shubhankar Srivastava demonstrates AutoBrowse, where a browser-operating agent and a teacher improve a persistent strategy file without updating model weights. The teacher reviews screenshots, trajectories, and outcomes after each attempt, preserving navigation lessons and shortcuts as a reusable skill. Flight-search and other examples show uneven progress: a passing iteration can be followed by failure, while successful runs can still improve on cost. The essential prerequisites are a replayable environment and a verifiable outcome. Q&A examines who evaluates the verifier, whether acceptable results are truly optimal, iteration budgets, skill portability, prompt injection, and changing websites. Monitoring and failure-triggered repair remain necessary after a skill graduates.
takeaways: Require replayable environments and explicit outcome criteria.
Evaluate verifier quality and define the optimization objective.
Monitor deployed skills for drift and review generated repairs.
reason: Core: evaluation-guided skill improvement, replay environments, outcome verifiers, and maintenance.

title: Let Your Agent Cook: Using Skills to Evaluate and Improve Your App — Ankur Duggal, Arize AI
summary: Ankur Duggal uses Arize CLI skills to bring operational traces, evaluations, annotations, and code into a coding agent’s repair workflow. A financial assistant’s plausible recommendations hide numeric-grounding problems, fabricated responses, repeated searches, and silent tool failures. The coding agent investigates these traces, proposes focused evaluators, and tests changes against datasets drawn from failing spans. An earlier international-stock experiment improves only after fixing both country context and an outdated tool, illustrating why prompt edits alone can be insufficient. The live repair remains unfinished at the end. The session recommends human review, application-specific rubrics, configurable judges, and sampling that balances ongoing quality monitoring with evaluation cost.
takeaways: Investigate trace-level causes before editing prompts.
Test repairs on datasets representing the original failures.
Review proposed fixes and evaluators; do not count an unfinished run as success.
reason: Core: application-specific evaluators and experiments for trace-driven agent repair.

title: 20 days of compute vs 7 hours: rethinking what state-of-the-art means — Bertrand Charpentier, Pruna
summary: Bertrand Charpentier challenges the idea of one universally best generative model. Public image-editing leaderboards disagree, aggregate rankings hide task-specific strengths, and personal inspection is biased by both reviewer preference and a few chosen samples. Automated metrics also require understanding and should match the target capability rather than serve as generic quality proxies. The talk recommends multiple benchmarks, realistic user conditions and larger samples, then adds latency, cost and energy to quality comparisons. Pareto plots expose several viable state-of-the-art choices and show why a small quality gain may not justify a large operational penalty.
takeaways: Evaluate the actual use case, not just an aggregate leaderboard rank.
Combine broader human review with understood, task-specific metrics.
Compare quality and efficiency on a Pareto frontier rather than choosing a single score winner.
reason: Model selection, metric validity and benchmarking methodology dominate the talk.
focus: Multidimensional model evaluation and Pareto analysis

title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
summary: Alvin Pane explains why disagreement with a production model is not automatically a regression: the production system can disagree with itself. In a synthetic HarborBite example, a cheaper candidate differs on eighteen percent of cases while repeated baseline runs differ on roughly seven percent. He combines telemetry, prefix caching, DSPy/GEPA prompt compression, and smaller-model experiments with shadow comparisons of baseline-to-baseline, candidate-to-candidate, and candidate-to-baseline behavior. Humans adjudicate disagreements into improvements, regressions, and ambiguity, then a paired confidence interval and critical-category checks inform release decisions. The reported prompt reduction illustrates the method, not realized million-dollar savings. Quality must still be monitored after deployment.
takeaways: Measure baseline nondeterminism before interpreting candidate disagreement.
Adjudicate improvements and regressions with humans.
Use paired confidence intervals and critical-category checks as release criteria.
reason: Core: statistical model-comparison methodology, shadow testing, and human adjudication.

title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
summary: Morgan Suo uses a financial research job to examine whether faster inference produces a faster usable result. M3.1 Flash changes include sparse attention, a lower-precision KV cache and experts, speculative decoding, serving-load choices, and reasoning budgets. Each optimization needs checks on retrieval, calculations, accuracy, and user-visible waiting time. She shows how average benchmark results can hide a task-specific regression, and how higher throughput can coincide with substantially worse tail latency. The proposed model-switch evaluation repeats the same research questions, checks sources and numbers, and counts retries and failed attempts in the total cost. The relevant unit is an acceptable completed report, not output tokens per second.
takeaways: Measure finished-task quality, latency, and total cost together.
Inspect category-level regressions and tail latency.
Include retries and failed attempts when comparing model configurations.
reason: Core: task-level quality and cost evaluation of model and inference changes.

title: The Cheaper AI Model That Costs You More - Rayan Krishnan, Vals AI
summary: Rayan Krishnan explains why aggregate model-card scores and advertised token prices are poor substitutes for task-specific evaluations. Vals AI benchmarks reveal a jagged frontier: model rankings change across finance tasks and even across subsets such as leveraged-buyout modeling. A nominally cheaper model can consume enough extra tokens to cost more per completed task. He discusses partial-credit versus fully-correct scoring, representative tasks, reliability, benchmark saturation, reward hacking, and multi-turn work. An internal-evaluation case study reportedly reduced a team’s token spending by about 90% while preserving useful output. He recommends converting an organization’s accumulated work into evaluation cases that encode its actual standards.
takeaways: Compare cost per completed task rather than price per token.
Inspect task subsets instead of trusting one aggregate leaderboard.
Build realistic multi-turn tests from historical work and guard against grader exploitation.
reason: Core: benchmark design, scoring validity, reward hacking, and internal model-selection evals.

title: LLM codegen fails and how to stop 'em — Danilo Campos, PostHog
summary: Danilo Campos analyzes failure modes in PostHog’s autonomous integration wizard and the interventions used to reduce them. Stale model knowledge is countered with current documentation, while lightweight reference applications show the intended integration shape. Staged instructions reduce unhelpful improvisation by separating discovery, event planning, and implementation. Crucially, an end-of-run question asks the agent what prevented success, exposing contradictory directives, unavailable tools, missing permissions, and language-mismatched guidance. Security examples replace unrestricted environment-file access with narrow key-presence and update tools. Q&A explains packaging reference applications and documentation as skill content. The emphasis is production feedback and error diagnosis, not a controlled benchmark or quantified causal evaluation.
takeaways: Use current documentation and compact reference integrations to counter stale model knowledge and inconsistent implementation patterns.
Ask agents after each run what would have better enabled success; the team reports finding contradictory instructions, inaccessible tools, and inappropriate language guidance this way.
Separate discovery, event planning, and implementation to reduce uncontrolled improvisation.
Diagnose privacy risks in tool behavior and expose narrowly scoped operations rather than sending raw environment-file contents to inference services.
reason: Failure analysis is the organizing subject, with concrete production errors and an ongoing end-of-run agent-feedback mechanism that revealed otherwise hidden harness and instruction problems. This fits core feedback/error analysis even though it offers no formal benchmark or calibrated judge. The security example further examines unintended behavior beyond nominal task success.
focus: Production agent feedback and failure analysis

title: Shipping complex AI applications — Braintrust & Trainline
summary: Braintrust and Trainline present a hands-on quality workflow for a staged support-triage agent. After adding deterministic tools and specialist stages, they instrument nested traces so reviewers can inspect inputs, outputs, tool calls, cost, and latency. A small golden dataset combines deterministic checks for structure and escalation policy with an LLM judge for nuanced customer-facing responses. Managed prompts, tools, and parameters support collaborative experiments and model comparisons. Online scoring monitors production traces, with sampling to control judge costs. The remediation exercise captures a misleadingly nonurgent invoice-export request, updates the prompt, and reruns evaluations, including regression checks. Trainline connects these practices to production model switching and travel-assistant reliability.
takeaways: Preserve a nested parent/child trace structure so failures can be localized to particular agent stages and tool calls.
Start with explicit expected behavior and edge cases; combine inexpensive deterministic scorers with LLM judges for genuinely nuanced criteria.
Apply online scoring to real production traces, using sampling to manage judge costs while retaining cheap deterministic checks.
Promote production failures into evaluation cases, compare the fix against a baseline, and rerun the wider suite to check for regressions.
reason: The workshop directly teaches a quality feedback loop: trace a multi-stage agent, build a golden dataset, implement deterministic and LLM scoring, compare experiments, score production traces, and remediate a concrete failure. Trainline supplies production context for evaluating model substitutions and customer-facing behavior. Observability is explicitly tied to diagnosing and improving quality.
focus: Offline and online evaluation, tracing, and failure remediation

title: Ralph Loops: Build Dumb AI Loops That Ship — Chris Parsons, Cherrypick
summary: Chris Parsons builds a Pomodoro application through repeated Claude Code runs that select and implement tickets, then expands the pattern to personal work and content generation. Quality depends on explicit feedback: tests, behavioral checks, screenshot inspection, simulated audience personas, and independent subagent or adversarial review. The Q&A highlights confirmation bias when an agent validates its own work, the risk that generated tests reproduce a misunderstood requirement, and continued human review for security-sensitive code. Parsons describes versioning prompts as skills but acknowledges that improvement remains subjective; proposed blind comparisons across ticket sets have not been performed. The workshop provides practical verification and feedback patterns rather than measured evidence that Ralph loops outperform alternatives.
takeaways: Specify how the loop verifies actual behavior; passing generated tests or marking a ticket complete is not sufficient.
Fresh-context subagents, adversarial review, and simulated audiences can provide different perspectives, but these examples do not establish calibrated evaluator accuracy.
Keep human closure and security-sensitive review where needed, and define explicit stop conditions for irreversible actions.
Prompt version control is not performance evaluation: Parsons acknowledges that he has not implemented objective comparative testing.
reason: The workshop ranges broadly over automation, but verification and feedback receive sustained practical treatment throughout the demonstration and Q&A: behavioral validation, screenshots, simulated personas, independent reviewers, self-confirmation bias, and the limits of subjective prompt improvement. This is substantive agent testing and feedback analysis, not merely a generic loop tutorial with an eval mention.
focus: Agent verification, independent review, and synthetic feedback loops

title: Demand-Driven Context: A Methodology for Coherent Knowledge Bases Through Agent Failure
summary: Raj Navakoti proposes using agent failures to discover missing enterprise knowledge rather than pushing an entire documentation collection into context. Agents attempt real work, identify unanswered domain questions, receive expert corrections, and preserve reusable context blocks. A workshop demonstration follows incident investigations and reports increasing confidence across fourteen iterations. A scanner extends the approach by generating probes from archived incidents, testing documentation, and classifying gaps, staleness, duplication, and priority. GitHub supplies review and versioning for curated Markdown. The Q&A limits the claims: testing was scoped to small teams, code and documentation can conflict, and maintaining correct, current knowledge remains unresolved. Confidence scores do not establish independently measured task accuracy.
takeaways: Use failed real tasks to identify specific missing context, then capture expert corrections for reuse instead of indiscriminately expanding retrieval.
Generate probes from archived incidents to assess documentation coverage and prioritize recurring, high-impact gaps.
Scope the process narrowly enough that domain experts can answer questions, and define precedence when code and documentation disagree.
Treat rising agent confidence as a diagnostic signal, not an independently validated accuracy result; knowledge freshness still requires oversight.
reason: Failure analysis and task-derived testing are central, not incidental: the workshop repeatedly exercises agents, extracts unmet information demands, generates knowledge probes, and uses gap classifications to drive corrections. The Q&A also probes validity, source conflicts, scale, and maintenance limitations.
focus: Failure-driven context evaluation and knowledge-gap analysis

title: Everything You Need To Know About Agent Observability — Danny Gollapalli & Zubin Koticha, Raindrop
summary: Raindrop's team argues that finite evaluation datasets cannot cover the expanding behavior of production agents. They propose monitoring explicit signals such as tool errors, latency, cost, and regenerations alongside semantic classifiers for refusals, task failure, and user frustration. Regex offers a cheap aggregate signal, while experiments compare issue rates between shipped variants and controls. The workshop adds a self-reporting tool to a coding agent, deliberately breaks file writing, and observes the agent report its bash workaround. Q&A covers sample-size limitations, historical backfills, clustering failures by use case, and exporting classified events. The speakers caution that self-diagnostics may miss behavior the model regards as successful.
takeaways: Track concrete issue categories and their rates instead of relying solely on generic numerical output ratings.
Compare production variants against controls using semantic failure signals, without confusing an early warning with statistical significance.
A neutral reporting tool and creator-feedback framing can elicit useful diagnostics, but self-reporting is not a dependable security verifier.
Cluster frustration and failure signals by task, tool, and trajectory to discover root causes and previously unknown regressions.
reason: The entire workshop concerns detecting, classifying, investigating, and experimentally reducing agent failures. It combines quality-related observability, controlled product comparisons, and a deliberately induced tool-failure demonstration, with Q&A on measurement limitations.
focus: Production agent quality monitoring and self-diagnostics
date_source: Reviewer-verified YouTube or publisher upload date

title: Feedback Loops are All You Need — Mehedi Hassan, Granola
summary: Mehedi Hassan describes Granola's move from one-shot chat features toward explicit feedback loops for improving AI product quality. Production problems include expensive, context-heavy web search, silent provider regressions, and summaries that miss different users' expectations. Granola built internal tracing that exposes tool calls, reasoning, search activity, and costs to product, data, support, and engineering staff. This lets teams investigate vague complaints and identify specific failures. The team also made its Electron renderer run as a web application, enabling per-PR previews and Cursor-driven checks with screenshots. The Q&A reports that experiments with Tauri had not produced meaningful performance gains.
takeaways: Expose complete agent traces in a usable interface so non-engineering teams can connect poor outputs to specific failures.
Monitor provider-dependent behavior: an upstream web-search update can degrade quality without an application deployment.
Make desktop frontends accessible through PR preview URLs to enable parallel human testing and automated agent verification.
reason: The central contribution is a quality-improvement loop built on trace inspection, production error diagnosis, and automated feature verification. The Electron work supports that testing loop rather than being an unrelated platform tour.
focus: Quality-focused tracing and AI product feedback loops
date_source: Reviewer-verified YouTube or publisher upload date

title: How we solved Context Management in Agents — Sally-Ann Delucia
summary: Sally-Ann Delucia explains how Arize's agent encountered runaway context growth while analyzing its own trace data. Naive truncation broke follow-up reasoning, while unconstrained summarization inconsistently discarded important information. The team instead preserved message heads and tails, retained recent tool results, and stored removed content for retrieval. A concrete testing method replays ten conversation turns and evaluates the eleventh to expose late-session failures before customers report them. Data-heavy searches move into subagents to protect the main conversation. The talk also acknowledges unresolved context-quality metrics and missing cross-session memory; the Q&A prioritizes long-term memory over cache-preservation work.
takeaways: Replay accumulated conversation history and evaluate a subsequent turn to catch failures that short, single-turn tests miss.
Treat broken follow-ups and forgotten context as observable failure modes when comparing context-management strategies.
The reported success of head/tail preservation plus retrieval is experiential; the team still lacks principled context-quality metrics.
reason: Includes a concrete long-session regression-testing method, analysis of observed reasoning failures, and discussion of how evals inform context selection. Although context engineering is the main framing, evaluation is operationally specified rather than merely mentioned.
focus: Long-session agent evaluation and context failure analysis

title: Malleable Evals: Why Are We Evaluating Adaptive Systems with Static Tests? — Vincent Koc, OpenClaw
summary: Vincent Koc argues that static evaluation suites calcify while agent behavior, harnesses, and user populations keep changing. He contrasts fixed offline question sets with adaptive testing and proposes outcome-oriented rubrics rather than exact-answer matching alone. Traces could supply automatically curated scenarios, always-on evaluations could detect changing use patterns, and telemetry-aware harnesses could respond to failures and cost constraints. His recurring stable-versus-changing workload example motivates maintaining the evolving edge cases instead of assuming a benchmark remains representative. The talk is conceptual: he says the intended implementation demonstration is not finished. Its contribution is an adaptive evaluation direction, not measured evidence that self-optimizing evaluation already works.
takeaways: Update evaluation coverage as production traces reveal changes in users, tasks, or agent behavior.
Define desired outcomes and suitable rubrics when multiple valid behaviors make exact-answer tests insufficient.
Connect telemetry and online quality assessment to the harness so observed failures can inform adaptation.
Treat the proposed self-curating evaluation system as a conceptual design, since the implementation demonstration was not ready.
reason: Evaluation design is the explicit subject throughout: limitations of static benchmarks, adaptive scenario selection, trace-derived suites, outcome rubrics, and quality-related telemetry. The transcript also clearly bounds the evidence by acknowledging that the planned demonstration is unfinished.

title: Mind the Gap (In your Agent Observability) — Amy Boyd & Nitya Narasimhan, Microsoft
summary: Boyd and Narasimhan connect agent observability to closing the gap between requirements and actual behavior as models, prompts, and environments change. Using a travel-agent example, they demonstrate OpenTelemetry tracing, trace-linked quality and safety evaluations, and agent-specific checks for intent resolution, task adherence, and tool calling. Their notebooks progress from a simple agent to specialist workflows, then batch evaluation and adversarial red-teaming scans. A preview observe skill generates evaluation data, establishes a baseline, analyzes failures, optimizes instructions, and compares versioned results. Further prompt changes cause regressions rather than perfect scores, prompting selection of an earlier best version. Audience discussion emphasizes human guidance, model-cost trade-offs, and reevaluation after changes.
takeaways: Link evaluation results to execution traces so a quality drop can be traced to specific tool calls, messages, or specialist agents.
Evaluate intent resolution, task adherence, and tool behavior alongside output quality and safety; rerun evaluations after model or prompt changes.
Use generated datasets and agent-assisted batch evaluation as a starting point, retain human guidance, and compare versioned results rather than assuming every optimization improves quality.
Complement ordinary quality and safety tests with adversarial scans for data leakage, instruction violations, and prohibited agent actions.
reason: Despite extensive Foundry setup and agent-building demonstrations, the session repeatedly connects tracing to quality diagnosis, implements batch quality/safety/agentic evaluations, demonstrates adversarial scanning, and uses measured regressions to select a better prompt version. Quality-linked observability and agent evaluation are central, so the combined talk is core rather than merely adjacent security or general platform engineering.

title: How to Leverage Domain Expertise — Chris Lovejoy, Notius Labs
summary: Lovejoy treats AI quality as an organizational problem: domain judgment must own assessment and feed concrete improvements. He distinguishes oracles, who inspect outputs and directly revise prompts; evaluators, who define metrics and failure taxonomies while engineers implement fixes; and architects, who design systems that learn from usage. Granola illustrates taste-driven review, Tandem illustrates decentralized clinical prompt ownership, and Anterior illustrates progression toward clinician review dashboards and automated adaptation. Choosing an organizational model depends on measurable outcomes, scale, and whether manual iteration is fast enough. He argues for a principal expert with ownership and complementary data-science or engineering skills rather than an advisory role without authority.
takeaways: Give a principal domain expert accountability and decision-making ownership for AI quality, rather than limiting experts to occasional advice.
Use direct expert review and prompt iteration when quality depends on taste; decentralize that ownership when specialties and customer needs diverge.
When outcomes are meaningfully measurable, define metrics and failure modes, collect expert reviews, and connect those findings to engineering fixes.
Move toward automated improvement only when manual iteration becomes inadequate; detailed experience with failures should inform the evaluation system.
reason: Although framed around organizational design, the talk substantively explains who defines quality, reviews outputs and traces, establishes failure modes and metrics, operates clinician review dashboards, and turns feedback into improvements. These are evaluation and feedback-system design concerns, not a general hiring talk with an incidental eval mention.

title: Fighting AI with AI — Lawrence Jones, Incident
summary: Lawrence Jones describes using coding agents to evaluate and debug Incident.io’s complex AI investigations. A small CLI lets agents inspect and edit individual YAML evaluation cases without loading enormous production examples into context. A runbook creates a failing case, adjusts the prompt, reruns regression checks, and simplifies accumulated instructions. To locate failures across many prompts, the team exports debugging interfaces and traces as self-documenting files alongside the codebase. For daily backtests, parallel agents analyze individual investigations before a clustering stage identifies shared failure patterns. This turns aggregate accuracy into actionable explanations and connects diagnosed problems to code changes that can be tested.
takeaways: Expose targeted evaluation operations through a CLI when large test fixtures overwhelm agent context.
Require a failing evaluation, a prompt fix, and checks that other cases still pass; periodically consolidate the prompt.
Export traces and debugging context as navigable files so agents can trace errors through the full prompt hierarchy.
Combine parallel per-investigation analysis with cohort clustering to explain quality changes that aggregate scores cannot explain.
reason: The entire talk concerns evaluating AI output, diagnosing errors in multi-prompt systems, maintaining regression datasets, and scaling quality analysis across customer investigations. The observability material is explicitly connected to locating failures and verifying fixes.
focus: Agent-assisted error analysis and regression evaluation

title: Harnesses in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
summary: Tejas Kumar builds a browser-agent harness around GPT-3.5 Turbo while keeping its prompt unchanged. The initial Hacker News task fails at authentication yet reports a successful upvote. He adds iteration limits, illustrative context trimming, bounded retries, and a deterministic verifier that inspects tool history for genuine success and unresolved login failures. A programmatic login handler then resolves authentication outside the model and records that intervention in the trace. The final demonstration checks the resulting page for an unvote option as confirmation. The lesson is to distinguish model claims from observed execution and encode explicit failure conditions before attempting to improve task completion.
takeaways: A model saying it finished is not sufficient evidence that its requested action occurred.
Deterministic verification should check tool results and explicit failure cases, including unrecovered authentication redirects.
Bound attempts and iterations, and manage context in the harness rather than relying entirely on prompting.
Verify externally visible state after execution; the demonstration confirms the upvote through the available unvote action.
reason: Although framed as harness engineering, a central worked example detects false success, implements deterministic outcome checks, exercises failure and recovery paths, and confirms the final external state. This directly addresses agent testing and verification rather than merely mentioning reliability.
focus: Deterministic agent verification and failure detection

title: How agent o11y differs from traditional o11y — Phil Hetzel, Braintrust
summary: Phil Hetzel contrasts uptime-oriented observability with measuring whether agents produce grounded, appropriate and useful behavior. Large semi-structured traces contain prompts, context and tool decisions needed for these qualitative assessments, creating different ingestion, indexing and query demands from ordinary application metrics. Domain experts such as clinicians and lawyers review traces and explain judgments; those rationales become scalable automated scorers. The talk connects real-time observability with batch evaluation on known inputs and describes clustering traces to discover intents, sentiment and previously unknown failures. Traditional technical metrics remain useful, but they do not establish functional agent quality.
takeaways: Instrument enough context to evaluate grounding and tool decisions.
Bring domain experts into trace review and capture their reasoning.
Use production failure discovery to populate offline experiments.
reason: Quality-focused observability, expert evaluation and failure discovery are central.
focus: Agent quality observability and human annotations

title: How Lovable self-improves every hour — Benjamin Verbeek, Lovable
summary: Benjamin Verbeek describes two continuous-improvement loops at Lovable. Session judges identify users who become stuck and later succeed; clustered solutions become contextual knowledge entries, reviewed and tested before injection. A small holdout receives blank injections, allowing production outcomes to determine whether entries help and whether stale advice should be removed. Separately, an agent vent tool reports missing capabilities, confusing instructions and broken platform behavior directly to engineers. Deduplicating agents investigate and propose fixes. Examples include file-copy failures involving spaces and incident-related feedback spikes, showing how inline agent feedback complements external conversation review.
takeaways: Use holdouts to verify that injected lessons improve real project outcomes.
Prune knowledge as models and product behavior change.
Give working agents a selective channel for concrete tool and platform failures.
reason: Judging, failure clustering, online controlled validation and continuous feedback are central.
focus: Production failure discovery and online validation

title: Task Fidelity Scaling Laws — Kobie Crawdord, Snorkel
summary: Kobie Crawford investigates whether better agentic tasks improve training outcomes under matched conditions. Terminal-Bench-style environments are accepted only if achievable, nontrivial, functionally correct and reliable. Accepted and rejected pools are compared through tool counts, pass rates, reasoning effort and failure categories before training with the same model, compute and task count. Higher-quality tasks produce cleaner capability failures and larger reported improvement. The discussion distinguishes genuine difficulty from underspecified instructions, hidden dependencies and mismatched tests. Human and LLM rubric agreement is also treated as a quality-control mechanism, particularly as tasks become less straightforwardly verifiable.
takeaways: Audit task executability and test/spec alignment before interpreting failure rates.
Compare training effects with model, compute and task count held fixed.
Use detailed failure taxonomies and human–judge agreement to validate task quality.
reason: Controlled study of task fidelity, evaluator quality and benchmark noise.

title: The Production AI Playbook: Deploying Agents at Enterprise Scale — Sandipan Bhaumik, Databricks
summary: Sandipan Bhaumik’s production playbook starts with measurable business success, representative expert cases and an evaluation pipeline before model selection. It distinguishes deterministic checks, semantic LLM judges and behavioral tests for tool use, loops and wasteful execution. A banking-chatbot case illustrates collecting evaluation data and tracing first, then detecting stale retrieval after a policy update through falling satisfaction and trace inspection. Evaluation datasets should grow from incidents, with ownership, categories and prompt-change provenance. The talk also discusses governance, orchestration and data foundations, but repeatedly ties them to observable quality, release validation and operational accountability.
takeaways: Define business targets and representative cases before selecting a model.
Evaluate tool behavior even when final answers are correct.
Govern a living incident-derived dataset and use smaller CI subsets when full runs are costly.
reason: Extensive evaluation architecture, LLM judges, behavioral checks and quality incident case study.

title: Production Evals For Agentic AI Systems - Nishant Gupta, Meta Superintelligence Labs
summary: Nishant Gupta reframes evaluation from scoring isolated model answers to measuring dependable agent workflows. Offline benchmarks remain useful, but scenario simulations and production telemetry reveal tool errors, retrieval and memory failures, recovery behavior and multi-agent coordination. He proposes continuous evaluation as a control-plane service that observes traces, runs simulations, coordinates targeted human review and feeds new cases into offline validation. Metrics map to outcomes: completion, tool success, escalation, safety violations, latency, cost and recovery. The talk emphasizes gradual drift across model, prompt, tool and user changes, making ongoing monitoring necessary rather than a single pre-release testing phase.
takeaways: Evaluate complete scenarios and recovery paths, not only answer accuracy.
Combine production traces with human calibration and offline update validation.
Treat evaluation as a continuous control-plane capability.
reason: Dedicated production evaluation architecture and reliability metrics.

title: User Signal Dies at the Retrieval Boundary - Sonam Pankaj, StarlightSearch
summary: Sonam Pankaj argues that traces and pass/fail evaluations are wasted if they never change the next agent run. Reflect adds runtime memory ranked by semantic similarity and historical usefulness: successful use increases utility and failed use reduces it. Reusable lessons can later become skills. The talk contrasts this with recency-only or similarity-only memory, reports company-run benchmark improvements, and demonstrates feedback changing a SQL product-search trajectory. It acknowledges cold starts, drifting utility and noisy review labels. The central contribution is an explicit connection from evaluation outcomes to retrieval behavior, rather than treating observability dashboards as the end of improvement.
takeaways: Make outcomes influence retrieval rather than merely recording them.
Distill recurrent successful reasoning into maintained skills.
Monitor label quality, cold starts and utility drift in feedback-driven memory.
reason: Evaluation-to-action feedback loop, trajectory inspection and benchmark validation.

title: Your Agent Failed in Prod. Good Luck Reproducing It. - Tisha Chawla & Susheem Koul, Microsoft
summary: Tisha Chawla and Susheem Koul distinguish reproducing a model output from replaying a failed system execution. Their Chronicle proof of concept records inputs, outputs and version metadata at semantic boundaries around model calls, tools and retrieval. A stock-selling example shows a valid API request executing the wrong quantity without raising errors. After adding a guardrail, recorded model outputs are replayed while the changed tool runs live, turning the original incident into an assertion-based regression test. The speakers separate deterministic tests of tools and guardrails from behavioral evaluations of tone or trajectory using judges.
takeaways: Record tool, memory and retrieval boundaries, not only prompts or network packets.
Replay unchanged nodes and execute the repaired component to test the exact failure.
Use behavioral evaluation alongside deterministic replay, not as its replacement.
reason: Failure reproduction, verification and regression methodology are central.

title: The Missing Layer After Launch - Raphael Kalandadze, Wandero AI
summary: Raphael Kalandadze describes an operational layer for agents after launch, where successful requests and green infrastructure metrics can conceal user-level failure. A short-cycle monitoring agent analyzes logs and code, proposes fixes and alerts; an independent review agent challenges whether each patch addresses a root cause. A separate session analyzer scores conversations and aggregates recurring problems, tool behavior and system health across customers. Browser-based testing supplies the user perspective missing from logs. The talk stresses access to traces, databases and interfaces, calibration of the operating agents, and keeping humans at review boundaries while making evidence understandable.
takeaways: Measure conversation outcomes, not just exceptions or request completion.
Separate local incident repair from cross-session failure discovery.
Combine trace analysis with user-facing browser checks and independent patch review.
reason: Production judging, quality observability and failure-driven testing are central.
focus: Production quality monitoring and agent-driven error analysis

title: Build AI Systems for Discernment, Not Approval - Angel Ortmann Lee, Duolingo
summary: Angel Ortmann Lee shows why human-in-the-loop review is not automatically reliable evaluation. In a Duolingo English Test experiment, experienced proctors accepted half of fabricated cheating alerts on legitimate historical sessions. Reframing instructions to require independent evidence improved rejection of false alerts from roughly 50% to 71%, without changing the model. The talk treats interaction design as part of the measurement system: distinguish detection from policy decisions, capture edits rather than only acceptance clicks, and expose assumptions in reviewable steps. Examples from tutoring and coding agents show how interfaces can generate useful labels or reinforce automation bias.
takeaways: Evaluate human reviewers under deliberately incorrect AI suggestions.
Separate model correctness from downstream policy decisions.
Capture structured corrections and disagreements, not only thumbs-up signals.
reason: Human judgment calibration and high-quality evaluation labels are central.

title: Your agent is blindfolded — Johan Lajili, Poolside AI
summary: Johan Lajili argues that the difference between successful and disappointing coding-agent use is often the feedback loop, not whether a repository is new or legacy. Poolside built an internal CLI that exposes its VS Code extension through screenshots, compact page snapshots, service logs, restarts, and higher-level interaction commands. This lets an agent reproduce a bug before changing code and verify the result afterward, rather than confidently reporting an untested intuition. Lajili frames agent-facing tooling and codebase accessibility as engineering work in their own right. He recommends inspecting repeated manual interventions and agent logs to discover the next missing observation or control.
takeaways: Require bug reproduction before accepting an agent’s diagnosis.
Give agents product-specific observation and interaction tools.
Use recurring manual checks and awkward log patterns to improve the testing interface.
reason: Substantial focus on agent self-testing, bug reproduction, and verification feedback.

title: Every Solo Agent Builder Eventually Reinvents a Worse Version of CI/CD - Sumaiya Shrabony
summary: Sumaiya Shrabony uses a 19-skill content pipeline to show how polished agent outputs can violate production contracts while declaring themselves ready. Her demonstration contrasts naive saving with blocking gates for voice drift, unsupported factual claims, and duplicated angles. The broader controls resemble established software practices: regression testing, scheduled-run monitoring, contract testing, staging, and audit trails. She recommends mapping every handoff, identifying where corrupted output is most costly, and adding a small boundary check there before expanding the agent system. A real gate must prevent downstream publication, not merely log a warning. The talk emphasizes observable failure paths and source-linked evidence over happy-path demos.
takeaways: Test handoff contracts as well as final artifact shape.
Block unsupported claims and duplicates before publication.
Start with the highest-cost failure boundary and retain an audit record.
reason: Direct agent regression/contract testing, failure demonstrations, and enforceable evaluation gates.
focus: Agent regression tests and output-contract gates

title: Stop AI Agent Hallucinations: 5 Techniques + Production Patterns - Elizabeth Fuentes, AWS
summary: Elizabeth Fuentes demonstrates five structural approaches to agent reliability using a toy travel assistant: semantic tool selection, graph-based retrieval, executor-validator-critic handoffs, code-enforced business rules, and runtime steering. Each section compares a baseline with a modified system, using known tool choices or booking outcomes to inspect errors, token use, and constraint compliance. The workshop distinguishes hard blocking from corrective feedback that lets an agent find an acceptable alternative. Its examples are explicitly dummy tools and small local demonstrations, not production-scale evidence for the headline performance claims. The useful evaluation pattern is to define observable failure cases and hold the surrounding task constant while testing a specific intervention.
takeaways: Compare interventions against explicit ground-truth cases and known constraints.
Validate tool failures independently instead of trusting a success narrative.
Separate hard invariant enforcement from soft-rule steering and measure task outcomes.
reason: Direct comparative failure-case testing, independent validation, deterministic guardrails, and error analysis.
focus: Comparative agent validation and hallucination controls

title: Medic for Apache Spark - First Aid for Failing Jobs - Drasko Profirovic, Pinterest
summary: Drasko Profirovic describes Pinterest’s Medic diagnostic agent and the evaluation infrastructure needed to improve it safely. Early manual tests depended on expiring production logs and made regressions difficult to identify. The team added OpenTelemetry traces and a record/playback harness: real tool responses are captured as versioned fixtures, replayed offline, and the resulting diagnostic reports graded against authored expectations. This turned quality changes into measurable regressions rather than anecdotes. Subsequent work improves exception retrieval, uses isolated visual analysis of metrics to control token volume, and separates specialist agents. The talk connects observability, reproducible inputs, targeted output rubrics, and architectural iteration in a concrete production support system.
takeaways: Snapshot real downstream responses into versioned fixtures for replay.
Grade diagnostic reports against explicit expectations and track regressions.
Use traces to distinguish bad reasoning from noisy or oversized tool context.
reason: Direct quality-linked observability, fixture-based offline evals, and agent regression-test harness.

title: From Signal to PR: Anatomy of a Self-Improving Agent — Jason Lopatecki, Arize
summary: Jason Lopatecki demonstrates Arize Signal as a loop connecting production telemetry to investigation and proposed fixes. Well-designed skills retrieve relevant traces, online-evaluation results, and logs into files beside the repository, giving coding agents concrete evidence of the executed path rather than a dashboard to navigate. Scheduled or event-triggered sandbox runs identify issues, build datasets or evaluators, and sometimes open a pull request. Lopatecki distinguishes scalable, predefined LLM judges from broader periodic agent investigations and says larger fixes still need human guidance. The key architectural concerns are composable data-access skills, security-conscious sandbox placement, and retaining enough telemetry to support evidence-backed diagnosis and review.
takeaways: Make traces and evaluation data accessible as files alongside code.
Convert recurring newly discovered failures into reusable evaluators.
Treat proposed fixes as evidence-backed review inputs, not proof of autonomous correctness.
reason: Quality-linked AI observability, online evaluation signals, and failure-to-fix feedback loop.

title: The Model Was Right. The Harness Failed. — Vinoth Govindarajan, OpenAI
summary: The talk argues that fluent model responses can conceal failures in the surrounding agent harness. Using public OpenClaw incidents, it examines delivered replies missing from durable history, concurrent writers losing updates, dangling tool calls, expired approvals, and messages accepted internally but never rendered. The proposed contract is that the model proposes, the harness commits, and durable receipts prove outcomes. Reliable systems assign each fact a replayable owner, serialize commits within shared state boundaries, bound waits and retries, and bind approvals to specific actions. A five-question audit checks triggers, inherited state, authority, execution, and surviving evidence, ending at the external result the user actually cares about.
takeaways: Distinguish message delivery from durable state persistence, and identify the owner and replay path for every retained fact.
Serialize mutations at each shared-state boundary while preserving parallel reads and independent work.
Give tools terminal outcomes and deadlines, and bind approval records to exact actions, arguments, and lifetimes.
Verify the user-visible or external side effect; a transcript or internal success flag is not sufficient proof.
reason: It focuses on production failure analysis and concrete audits that verify agent state, authorization, execution, and externally observable outcomes.

title: Designing Agents (The Floor Is the Frontier) — Ben Hylak, Raindrop
summary: Ben Hylak distinguishes maximizing frontier benchmark capability from raising an application's reliability floor. He argues that brittle chatbot-era datasets and exact tool-call expectations often fail when models or harnesses change, so offline agent evaluations should increasingly resemble executable unit and end-to-end tests kept as code. Production improvement requires discovering unknown issues, identifying when each began, and measuring affected users. He cautions that trace clusters are not stable issue definitions: broad groups can mix unrelated root causes and are difficult to track over time. Instead, he recommends scalable code-based classifiers and deterministic anomaly signals, with agents investigating detected changes rather than being asked to discover anomalies unaided.
takeaways: Evaluate the full agent harness with tests as code rather than treating a prompt string as the whole system.
Track issue onset and user prevalence to connect regressions with changes and prioritize repairs.
Do not equate semantic clusters with durable, actionable issue categories.
Detect changes using tractable deterministic signals, then use agents to investigate the evidence.
reason: Focuses on production-quality monitoring, actionable issue analysis, and practical offline evaluation of changing agent systems.
focus: Production issue detection and agent quality monitoring

title: Improving Agents is a Data Mining Problem — Vivek Trivedy, LangChain
summary: Vivek Trivedy frames agent improvement as a data loop: deploy, collect complete traces, mine behavior, and run experiments on prompts, tools, orchestration, or models. Traces expose user dissatisfaction, post-compaction degradation, and behavioral differences that aggregate scores obscure. Because long traces are expensive and may exceed context windows, analysis agents should query them as external data rather than ingest everything. Curated outputs support evaluation datasets, training examples, and human review. He describes starting with strong models, testing cheaper open models, and using harness engineering before fine-tuning when returns plateau. Dense diagnostic feedback from traces is presented as more useful for automated improvement than a bare benchmark pass/fail signal.
takeaways: Centralize tool calls, messages, and execution data so agent behavior can be inspected across production runs.
Mine traces into concrete failure cases and evaluation datasets, then test proposed changes against them.
Query large traces selectively and benchmark cheaper judging models on the actual domain task.
Provide diagnostic evidence beyond pass/fail, and try fast-feedback harness changes before escalating to fine-tuning.
reason: Explains how production traces become error-analysis evidence, evaluation datasets, and feedback for experimentally verified agent improvements.
focus: Trace mining and evaluation-driven error analysis

title: Your Agent Evolved. Your Evals Didn't. — Ameya Bhatawdekar, Braintrust
summary: Ameya Bhatawdekar argues that evaluation must evolve with agent architecture rather than remain attached to an application's earliest design. Using an SRE agent as a running example, he traces the progression from single model calls through retrieval chains, workflow graphs, autonomous loops, and systems augmented with memory, execution sandboxes, and skills. Each transition introduces new failure surfaces, requiring checks beyond final-answer correctness, including retrieval, node contracts, tool use, branching, and retries. For variable agent trajectories, he recommends repeated runs and distributional metrics separating capability from reliability. He closes with a production-to-evaluation flywheel and Braintrust's clustering-based Topics feature for discovering previously unanticipated failure categories and building fresh regression datasets.
takeaways: Update evaluation coverage whenever architectural changes introduce new tools, memory, orchestration, or execution components.
Evaluate intermediate nodes and contracts as well as end-to-end outcomes when workflows can fail between steps.
Repeat nondeterministic tasks to distinguish occasional success from reliable behavior across runs.
Cluster production traces to discover unknown failure types, then convert them into maintained regression cases.
reason: Included because it directly explains how evaluation units, metrics, and failure-discovery practices should change as agent systems evolve.
focus: Architecture-aware agent evaluation and production failure discovery

title: Agents Are Where Microservices Were in 2015 — Roberto Milev & Uday Kanagala, Navan
summary: Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala outline production agent infrastructure at Navan, with a substantial focus on debugging and evaluating nondeterministic behavior. They use skills as independently testable context units and hooks around tool calls to emit traces of goals, decision signals and execution. Instead of asserting one fixed sequence or exact output, they discuss trajectory evaluations that measure progress toward the intended goal, completeness and efficiency. Inferred answers can trigger human review, and regressions inform fixes. The talk also covers identity, authorization and orchestration, recommending a manageable single-agent foundation before multi-agent complexity. Its evaluation contribution links operational traces, component boundaries and trajectory-based testing.
takeaways: Test reusable skill units separately from complete agent workflows.
Instrument decision and tool boundaries for actionable quality traces.
Score goal progress and trajectory quality rather than assuming a deterministic execution graph.
reason: Significant dedicated sections on trajectory evals, regressions and observability tied to quality.
focus: Agent trajectory testing and quality observability

title: An AI Research Agent That Runs Your Experiments — Tim Sweeney, Weights & Biases
summary: Sweeney demonstrates ARIA as a research assistant that queries experiment history, builds reports and visualizations, and launches GPU-backed code and hyperparameter experiments through Weights & Biases. A live batch runs twelve experiments but does not beat the prior best loss, illustrating iteration without guaranteed improvement. He then explains ARIA's development loop: production tracing and online judges reveal behavioral issues, which become YAML tasks scored for correctness, insight quality, and tool-call efficiency in nightly evaluations. Candidate-versus-production dashboards guide releases. He recommends agent-oriented observability, evaluation-driven go/no-go decisions, domain context, and human trace review because model judges miss nuances. The agent complements researchers rather than replacing hypothesis-setting and judgment.
takeaways: Connect production behavioral failures to explicit offline evaluation tasks.
Score correctness, usefulness, and efficiency rather than execution alone.
Keep human review and accept that experimental batches may not improve results.
reason: Substantial treatment of research-agent observability and nightly evaluations. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: How We Built an Agent That Improves Itself — Zubin Aysola, Weights & Biases
summary: Aysola explains how Weights & Biases develops ARIA through a production-to-simulation evaluation loop rather than relying primarily on reinforcement learning. Research and production use identical agent code, synchronized regularly to reduce drift. Tasks define starting environments and desired outcomes, including single prompts and simulated multi-turn users; scoring combines task completion with relative behavioral comparisons. Production failures and successful patterns become offline tasks, and product teams assess benchmark relevance. A live example converts a trace into a regression case, compares candidate and production variants, and targets an SDK logging error through prompting or skills. He stresses thoughtful measurement despite automation; the demonstration does not establish a broad improvement magnitude or eliminate the need to validate evaluation relevance.
takeaways: Minimize production-simulation drift with shared code and synchronized environments.
Turn real traces into repeatable tasks and compare candidate against production.
Automation does not replace judgment about scoring robustness and meaningful improvement.
reason: Substantial treatment of production-derived agent evaluations. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Why 99% Accurate Browser Agents Still Fail — Derek Meegan, Browserbase
summary: Meegan explains why reliable browser automation requires more than strong per-step model accuracy: transactional workflows accumulate risk and cost but deliver value only when completed. He distinguishes browser representations and autonomy levels, then prioritizes task performance before cost and maintainability. Success should be verified through concrete artifacts such as receipts or queryable records and measured per transaction, including retries, rather than per run alone. A health-insurance portal architecture moves stable authentication and downloading into deterministic functions, adds document verification against records, and reserves agent reasoning for genuine ambiguity guided by skills. His probability examples are illustrative assumptions, while observability and reevaluation remain necessary as sites, tasks, and models change.
takeaways: Verify concrete transaction outcomes instead of accepting agent declarations.
Reduce probabilistic steps by extracting stable operations into tools.
Measure transaction-level reliability and maintain reevaluation as environments change.
reason: Substantial treatment of browser-agent reliability and outcome measurement. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Your LLM App Returned 200 OK. It Was Still Wrong. — Marina Petzel, Datadog
summary: Petzel argues that traditional latency, error, traffic, and saturation monitoring remains necessary but cannot establish generative-AI application health. Successful HTTP responses can conceal hallucinations, unsafe disclosures, or irrelevant answers, while model choices and context growth make costs variable. She proposes cost attribution by feature, user, model/provider, and environment, alongside attention to caching and token creep. Safety monitoring covers injection attempts, personal-data leakage, toxic content, and jailbreaks. Quality monitoring combines groundedness checks, relevance, user feedback, completeness judgments, and retrieval metrics, using both automation and manual review. Datadog is offered as an implementation platform; numerical targets and spending examples are presenter recommendations or claims rather than validated universal thresholds.
takeaways: Add cost, safety, and semantic quality monitoring to infrastructure metrics.
Tag spending dimensions to locate expensive features and usage patterns.
Combine human review, task-specific metrics, and automated checks rather than trusting HTTP success.
reason: Substantial treatment of production quality monitoring. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 201 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Voss extends agent observability from manually reading traces to automated improvement driven by evaluations and recurring failure patterns. Because identical inputs can follow different paths, he treats aggregated traces as behavioral evidence and evaluator explanations as actionable feedback. A toy-store workshop instruments an application, analyzes searches, and adds missing price filtering; the coding agent copies a nearby pre-solved implementation, limiting the demonstration's independence. Arize Signal is presented as a scheduled trace-analysis agent that suggests issues, datasets, evaluators, and reviewable fixes. He emphasizes regression evaluations to preserve existing behavior and describes Signal's own internal evaluations and judges. Autonomous evaluator creation is not enabled, and suggestions still require user decisions.
takeaways: Use trace-derived failure clusters to prioritize improvements at scale.
Run regression evaluations before accepting automated fixes.
Evaluate improvement agents themselves and retain reviewable evidence.
reason: Substantial treatment of agent evaluation and automated error analysis. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.
focus: Agent evaluation and automated error analysis

title: Advanced Workshop: Mastering AI Observability — Doug Guthrie, Braintrust
summary: Guthrie demonstrates an observability-to-evaluation improvement loop using a support agent, Braintrust tracing, online judges, and topic clustering. He distinguishes deterministic checks from subjective model judges and stresses human calibration, difficult examples, and evolving datasets. Topics preprocess conversations, summarize facets, embed them, and cluster patterns to expose issues beyond existing scores. The workshop imports example traces, configures scoring scope and sampling, then uses SQL-capable coding agents to investigate failures, create regression cases, modify code, and compare evaluations. Limitations remain explicit: demonstration data is synthetic, a built-in issues facet produces insufficient matches, Topics requires hosted models, and reviewers must assess generated changes. Network problems also prevent normal audience participation.
takeaways: Trace intermediate steps and calibrate judges with human review.
Combine known-failure scores with clustering to discover untested behavior.
Scope multi-turn scoring correctly and budget online sampling costs.
Require evaluation evidence and human review for automated improvement PRs.
reason: Substantial treatment of ai observability and evaluation workshop. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Why Building an Eval Platform Is Harder Than It Looks — Braintrust
summary: Braintrust's presenter explains why an evaluation platform grows far beyond a spreadsheet and results interface. Early loops execute examples and record scores; later stages add collaborative review, nontechnical experimentation, and side-by-side prompt or model comparisons. The crucial next step links production observability to offline regression datasets so real failures drive improvement without new regressions. Supporting this requires ingesting large, nested traces, querying fresh and historical data, preserving snapshots, and managing permissions and masking. He describes Braintrust's query abstraction and agent-assisted failure discovery as responses to those systems demands. Humans still choose what to ship; automated insight capabilities are presented as product direction and functionality, not independently benchmarked guarantees.
takeaways: Turn production failures into reusable offline regression cases.
Plan for trace storage, query workloads, governance, and cross-role collaboration.
Agent-driven experimentation does not remove human release responsibility.
reason: Substantial treatment of evaluation platforms and production feedback. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
summary: Blanes frames reliable browser agents as a customer-feedback problem rather than a contest to maximize static benchmark scores. Drawing on Amazon’s Nova service rollout, he proposes a flywheel: define success in customer terms, capture telemetry and direct conversations, diagnose model, engineering, or product gaps, and prioritize changes. Customer needs evolve from discovery through early adoption and scale, so evaluation scenarios must evolve too. He describes an observed trust cliff between roughly 80% and 92% reliability, not a universal safety threshold. Examples include trajectory caching, nontechnical QA tooling, and customization. Honest communication of limitations and out-of-scope capabilities is presented as essential to trust.
takeaways: Build scenarios from production behavior and customer conversations.
Separate research, engineering, and product failures before prioritizing.
Disclose limitations instead of presenting benchmark scores as guarantees.
reason: Substantial treatment of customer-centered evaluation flywheel. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: Continuously Improving Agents with Langfuse — Annabell Schäfer & Lotte Verheyden, ClickHouse
summary: Schäfer and Verheyden present an AI engineering loop connecting production tracing and monitoring with offline datasets, experiments, and regression checks. Their workshop instruments a dad-focused IT support agent and configures semantic judges for disagreement and out-of-scope requests alongside a deterministic all-caps frustration check. They emphasize selecting application-specific failure signals rather than copying generic evaluators. A coding agent then analyzes seeded traces, surfacing retrieval failures, retry costs, and monitoring coverage gaps. The practical focus remains online observability; the broader recommendation is to maintain representative datasets and evaluation criteria continuously, with human review catching novel failures that automated checks can miss.
takeaways: Capture useful trace context before designing evaluations.
Combine deterministic checks, semantic judges, and human feedback.
Turn production failures into maintained regression datasets.
