reason: Substantial treatment of quality observability and feedback loops. Direct application/agent-quality evaluation content.

title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava, New York Life & Tanmay Sah
summary: Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah study 1,368 public AI incidents to derive a broader evaluation framework. They organize failures across technical strength, deployment controls, and business context, with thirteen subdimensions reportedly covering about ninety-eight percent of the incidents examined. Human oversight, monitoring, authority, assumptions, and material business harm matter alongside model accuracy. Their proposed build-break-fix loop deliberately searches for counterexamples rather than confirming that a system works. An airline chatbot’s incorrect refund advice illustrates how a narrow model test misses consequential system-level failures. They also stress evaluating the evaluator itself, since generated tests and AI judges can reproduce blind spots instead of providing independent evidence.
takeaways: Prioritize evaluation according to business risk and system authority.
Test deployment controls and harm detection, not just model quality.
Seek falsifying cases and verify the evaluator’s assumptions.
reason: Core: incident-derived failure taxonomy and risk-based evaluation of complete AI systems.

title: Your Agent Fix Just Broke Something Else - Sofia Jakovcevic, Arize AI
summary: Sofia Jakovcevic demonstrates why a prompt fix can improve one behavior while degrading another: an illustrative support-agent change raises action safety by seventeen points but lowers task completion by seventeen. Her five-step regression loop starts with production traces, curates representative successes and failures, defines evaluators, runs a baseline, compares one change, and gates merges in CI. The workshop shows prompt-level and full-agent experiments with outcome scores, latency, cost, and errors. Coding agents can consume the same traces and evaluation artifacts to investigate problems, but proposed repairs still need testing. Each new production failure should enrich the regression suite rather than disappear after a one-off patch.
takeaways: Protect existing successes as well as known failure cases.
Compare multiple quality dimensions against a fixed baseline.
Make evaluation results enforceable merge criteria and keep adding production failures.
reason: Core: regression datasets, multi-metric experiments, and evaluation gates in CI.

title: What Does an AI Engineer Do Now? - Aparna Dhinakaran, Arize AI
summary: Aparna Dhinakaran argues that AI engineering is shifting from implementing individual features to building feedback loops around fleets of agents. Arize Signal illustrates an always-on agent that reads telemetry, remembers prior issues, and proposes changes, with durable state surviving disposable sandboxes and failures. Evaluation is necessary at several levels: offline tests of a proposed repair, human-aligned golden datasets for the evaluators themselves, and online checks of production behavior. She emphasizes that agents increasingly consume observability data directly, making trace quality part of the improvement system. The talk connects scheduling, triggers, persistent memory, and model-independent harnesses to reliable evaluation rather than treating monitoring as a dashboard added after deployment.
takeaways: Design telemetry for automated investigation as well as human inspection.
Evaluate proposed changes offline and behavior online.
Test evaluators against human-labeled golden data.
reason: Core: observability and evaluator calibration as the foundation of continuous agent improvement.

title: Agents That Self Improve While You Sleep - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
summary: Fuad Ali demonstrates a self-improvement loop in which production traces become issues, datasets, evaluators, experiments, and proposed repairs. Signal periodically reviews a shopping agent’s traces, remembers earlier findings to avoid duplicates, and diagnoses a category-formatting bug from evidence rather than an implausible final answer alone. Failures are preserved as regression cases and replayed against a candidate fix. The workshop compares code checks, LLM judges, and decision models, and discusses evaluation health, qualitative output, sampling, and cost. Humans retain leverage over rubric design, dataset curation, and reviewing changes. The useful distinction is between detecting a production problem and experimentally establishing that a repair resolves it without introducing regressions.
takeaways: Turn production failures into persistent regression cases.
Test proposed fixes against the same cases and evaluators.
Keep humans responsible for evaluation intent and review evaluation costs.
reason: Core: full tracing-to-failure-analysis-to-evals-to-experiments improvement loop.

title: Skill Issue: How We Used AI to Make Agents Actually Good at Supabase — Pedro Rodrigues, Supabase
summary: Pedro Rodrigues walks through evaluating agent skills against Supabase database tasks. A performance-review application exposes how a seemingly successful generated SQL view can bypass row-level security. Adding a security skill changes the generated migration to include security_invoker, but the live application still has other vulnerabilities. The workshop then compares skill and no-skill conditions using a reset database, headless Claude Code, and deterministic assertions. A faulty evaluator marks similar outputs differently, demonstrating why graders themselves need inspection. The speaker distinguishes appending skill instructions to the system prompt from organic discovery and recommends representative triggering and non-triggering scenarios, isolated environments, regression checks, and maintaining only relevant production skills.
takeaways: Specify expected behavior and representative scenarios before grading a skill, including when it should and should not activate.
Compare skill and no-skill runs from the same reset state; use isolated environments to avoid contamination from unrelated installed skills.
Validate graders against actual generated artifacts: a faulty assertion can report failure even when the requested security setting is present.
Do not infer reliable security improvement from a changed SQL flag or a single run; the live demo retained vulnerabilities and the final compared outputs were similar.
reason: The workshop explicitly teaches evaluation design, controlled skill ablations, deterministic versus LLM judging, trigger tests, reproducible state, and regression checks. Security is the example task, but the main contribution is core agent-testing methodology, including an instructive evaluator failure rather than a proven performance gain.
focus: Agent skill evaluation, grader validation, and security regression testing

title: Combine Skills and MCP to Close the Context Gap — Pedro Rodrigues, Supabase
summary: Pedro Rodrigues explains Supabase’s evaluation-driven development of an agent skill. A matched task shows why tool access alone is insufficient: creating a PostgreSQL view without security_invoker can bypass existing row-level security, while the skill-guided agent handles the constraint. He describes six project scenarios tested across four models under three conditions: neither MCP nor skills, MCP alone, and MCP plus the skill. The combined condition leads on the reported task-completeness measure. Observed failures also shape the document: security essentials belong in the main skill because references may be skipped, while changing documentation should be linked. Q&A addresses repository-based distribution and unresolved packaging limitations.
takeaways: Compare controlled agent configurations on realistic project scenarios rather than assuming tool access guarantees correct behavior.
The reported experiment compares a no-MCP/no-skill baseline, MCP alone, and MCP plus a skill; it does not establish a skill-only condition.
Check environment-specific security behavior, such as whether a view preserves row-level security, instead of checking only task completion.
Use observed agent behavior to decide which critical constraints must be directly present in the main skill file.
reason: The talk includes a concrete security failure comparison and a described multi-model, three-condition evaluation across six scenarios. Those experiments and failure observations materially inform the skill design, making the agent-evaluation content more substantial than a passing benchmark score.
focus: Agent skill evaluation and security verification

title: Can LLMs generate Enterprise Quality Code? — Prasenjit Sarkar, Sonar
summary: Prasenjit Sarkar presents Sonar’s analysis of thousands of Java programming assignments across dozens of models. Functional benchmark scores are placed alongside code volume, bug density, security findings and cyclomatic or cognitive complexity to show why passing tests does not establish enterprise readiness. The talk compares model behaviors and warns that more recent models can produce substantially more code and subtler issues. title: Evals-Driven Development for a Mental Health AI Coach — Akele Reed & Dave Revere, SonderMind
summary: Akele Reed and Dave Revere describe a mental-health coach whose independent input and output guardrails are calibrated through clinician-led evaluation. The goal is not maximal intervention: inappropriate escalation can itself deny support, while indirect crisis language may evade generic moderation. Licensed clinicians annotate traced conversations with expected observations, categories, and the turn where intervention should occur. title: We Vetted 2000 AI Skills Before They Reached Developers — Lucas Palma, Nubank
summary: Lucas Palma describes Nubank's security-review pipeline for AI skills, treating instructions, plugins, and MCP integrations as supply-chain dependencies rather than harmless configuration. Developers can scan locally, but mandatory CI rescans submissions before internal marketplace distribution. Deterministic pattern checks handle clear risks, while LLM review adds behavioral context; findings appear in pull requests and machine-readable security reports. title: Teaching AI to Find Real Vulnerabilities — Prof. David Brumley, Bugcrowd
summary: Brumley explains cybersecurity evaluation through two ladders: target difficulty and exploitation capability. He argues that single-bug tasks and crash-only rewards encourage agents to rediscover easy flaws or overstate hacking ability. His audit-task alternative accepts multiple executable proofs, deterministically validates and deduplicates vulnerabilities, and balances precision with recall while expanding ground truth for newly discovered bugs. He then presents a staged V8 evaluation separating crashes, memory-access primitives, sandbox escape, and code execution. Across 41 verified vulnerabilities, Brumley reports code-execution success of 73% for Mythos and 68% for GPT, contrasting with much easier crash triggering. takeaways: Require executable proofs and deterministic grading instead of accepting an agent's claim that it found or exploited a vulnerability.

Separate crash detection from stronger exploitation capabilities; coarse success definitions can conceal large differences between models.

title: Guardrails First: Engineering Member-Facing Health AI — Rashi Agrawal, Hinge Health
summary: Rashi Agrawal describes member-facing healthcare AI as an architectural safety problem, not something solved by stronger prompts. Production safety combines continuously running multidimensional judges, member feedback, and human trace review, with every high-stakes case checked. Combine live automated scoring with member feedback and human review, including all high-stakes traces.
Validate a judge's finding before modifying agent behavior; judges themselves require maintenance.
Assess launch-blocking severity by plausible harm, not available capacity, and make risk acceptance explicit.

title: Loophole: Adversarial Agents To Stress Test Your Morality — Brendan Rappazzo, Morgan Stanley
summary: Brendan Rappazzo presents Loophole, a personal open-source project that stress-tests moral rules using adversarial agents. title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
summary: Corey Gallon describes three levels of review for agents that misstate completion, extract facts incorrectly, or reason from faulty assumptions. title: From Tokens to Cells: Foundation Models for Single-Cell Biology - Akram Baharlouei, Altos Labs
summary: Akram Baharlouei surveys single-cell foundation models and the measurement problems that complicate their evaluation. summary: Uri Rolls and Thom Wolf present an access-control benchmark built from previously undisclosed vulnerabilities found by human researchers. title: State of Data — Sean Cai, Independent / State of Data

title: Should AI Engineers Still Read Code in 2026? The Z/L Continuum — Alex Volkov, ThursdAI
